title: Tornado leaves 'devastating' trail of damage in Ulladulla
text:
A tornado that ripped through the CBD of Ulladulla on the NSW South Coast on Saturday has left homes uninhabitable and severe damage in its wake.

The State Emergency Service (SES) said the tornado, which reached a wind-gust front of 98 kilometres per hour about 1pm, impacted 15 properties.

More than half a dozen were severely damaged and two of them deemed uninhabitable, the residents forced to relocate to the homes of friends and family.

SES Deputy Incident Commander Tracy Provest said it had a "devastating" impact.

The NSW State Emergency Service responded to 34 reports of damage in Ulladulla. (Supplied: Edwin Fletcher)

"We've had quite a number of homes where walls are gone or the roof has peeled off or tiles are on the other side of the road," she said.

" We've had trees down come through houses. "

Street signs were also torn out of the ground and uprooted trees and falling branches fell on cars.

"Amazingly, nobody was injured," Ms Provest said.

"Even the couple of trees that came down on cars, the people who were in the cars managed to get out.

" [One] lady was across the road buying fish and chips and she watched a tree come down on her car. She was so thankful that she wasn't in it. "

Loading...

Ms Provest said she had never seen anything like it.

"I've been here since 2003, and I think for a lot of people who live locally, this is definitely a first," she said.

"One fellow had a small tinny on a trailer at the front of his house, it flipped the tinny off the trailer, lifted the trailer and knocked it into his car."

The tornado ripped roofs off homes, leaving two uninhabitable. (Supplied: NSW SES Ulladulla)

The service received 34 calls for help within Ulladulla, with most jobs finalised by Sunday afternoon after crews from as far as Yass were called in as back-up.

Across the state, 438 calls for assistance were received in the 24-hour period.

The town also received 24 millimetres of rain between 9am on Saturday and 9am on Sunday.

SES crews worked across Saturday afternoon and Sunday morning to repair damage to several homes and businesses. (Supplied: SES)

Local captures vision of tornado

Brad Collins was driving in town with his father when he saw the storm unfold and captured a video on his smart phone as the clouds formed into a vortex.

"It developed around us and it was that quick, the next minute it was in front of us," he said.

" There was stuff flying in the air … then it was all over. "

He described it as "surreal" and "crazy", later driving past several homes with roofs torn off and one car crushed by a tree.

CCTV from a local cafe showed heavy rain and strong winds sweep through violently, sending umbrellas flying into the harbour.

Loading...

The Bureau of Meteorology said the tornado was classified as "sub-severe" but was a unique event.

"For the coast of New South Wales, it's quite unusual to see tornadoes like that," meteorologist Tristan Sumarna said.

"Even though it was sub-severe, there was definitely some impact."

SES volunteers from the Ulladulla unit and across the state responded to the damage. (Supplied: NSW SES Ulladulla)

Ms Provest praised the local clean-up effort, saying Shoalhaven Council and NSW Police assisted with the roads as well as traffic direction, while multiple volunteers pitched in.

"A couple were directly impacted, and other had businesses impacted, and they've all been out helping anyway," she said.

Festival paused for storm

A 2-hour drive north, in Wollongong, the Yours and Owls Festival at Flagstaff Hill was briefly paused when the storm rolled in on Saturday evening.

Festival-goers told the ABC they were directed to seek shelter under tents for about 20 minutes.

Victoria Schuck was in the crowd and said despite the interruption, they made the most of it, holding a sing-a-long under the tents before the show went on.

"I think it added to it; it gives you a good story to tell and it was a lot of fun," she said.

title: Tragedy will drive Knights to bring home NRL trophy, fans say
text:
Fans say the tragedy at Newcastle where 10 people were injured after a car crashed into Knights supporters will only make the team "work harder" to bring the NRL trophy home.

Thousands of supporters have descended on Stadium Australia decked out in red, blue and white as they eagerly await their team battling it out against the Sydney Roosters for NRL grand final glory.

Last year, the team claimed the wooden spoon, and today's grand final appearance is their first in 25 years.

It has been 25 years since the Knights have played in a grand final. (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

Adding to the emotion of the day was the incident at a roundabout on Newcastle Link Road, at Wallsend, impacting fans lining the road to farewell the team bound for the stadium.

Six people remain in hospital, with a five-year-old girl among two people in a serious but stable condition.

Charlotte Barker and Mitchel Eastwood arrived in Sydney yesterday.

Ms Barker told the ABC it was "really sad" when they found out about what had happened, but being there today was "unreal".

"It's been good news this morning that she's [5-year-old girl] is back in a stable condition," she said.

"It was really hard to feel positive yesterday, but I think, yeah, it feels good today. There's good vibes around."

Ms Barker says it was hard to feel positive yesterday. (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

Mr Eastwood said he was confident of a Newcastle win, adding: "Hopefully the boys can get up for all those people ... I'm sure they will."

The sentiment was shared by a group of excited supporters, who were predicting the game would be a "white wash", saying it would "mean everything".

"It's our time ... you can't measure heart, we've just got ticker," a friend said.

" That's [the incident] just going to drive the boys more, it's going to drive the boys to work harder and bring that trophy home for the town. "

Fans told the ABC they were confident of a Newcastle win. (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

Trish said she would not let the accused driver "take the joy of the day".

"Look at us all, we're all the for the boys today," she said.

"And the boys will be there for the [injured] and we'll be there for them when we get back home."

Trish has been a Knights fan "from day dot", and was "just so proud", watching them take home the premiership title in 1997 and 2001.

"So this third one, we're gonna win also," she added.

Trish says she has been a fan of the Knights since " day dot". (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

A father with two young boys said it was "devastating" to see all those people injured, but was glad they were "recovering well".

"I'm just hoping for a great performance from the team and everything, hope we can get the job done," one of the boys said.

He added: "If we get the job done for them and make this city proud."

Roosters fan, Blake Allen, while adamant that his team would be victorious, also recognised the "Newcastle spirit".

"Terrible incident ... but you can see right now there's five to one Newcastle fans, so I think they're all gonna rally behind this," he said.

"And if anything, I think this will help Newcastle lift and make for an even better grand final."

Fans say a win will help lift the town. (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

Newcastle mayor Gavin Morris posted a video on social media.

"We can grieve for those that were hurt and injured in yesterday's incident, and we can support our might Knights who have gone through so much as well," he said.

"They endured a lot through their trip to Sydney, getting the news through of what happened, but today right now I say to the boys, it's time now to get out there and give it your best."

An 18-year-old Sydney man has been refused bail after being charged over the crash.

title: 'Debris field' found in search for missing medical flight from Bermuda
text:
Searchers have found debris from an air ambulance that was carrying six people when it went missing over the Atlantic during a flight from Bermuda to Boston.

The "debris field" was found off the coast of Nantucket, in the US state of Massachusetts, following the disappearance on Saturday, the US Coast Guard said.

Four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals were aboard, the Coast Guard said in a statement.

It added that the next of kin of those missing had been notified and one of its cutters would keep searching the water overnight and into Sunday.

According to the Coast Guard, the Federal Aviation Administration reported that the Gulfstream G100 aircraft lost contact very early on Saturday morning.

Air traffic audio indicates that it may have been "coming in blind" when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it disappeared.

The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net.

"Roger, you said you're coming in blind. Is that what you said?" a controller can be heard asking the pilot.

The plane may have lost its navigational instruments as a storm seen on radar moved across its path, former US Department of Transportation inspector-general Mary Schiavo said.

The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 7.3 kilometres to around three kilometres, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.

"Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm," Ms Schiavo, an aviation attorney, said.

"It's a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind.

"It's very easy to get disoriented and not know if you're turning, climbing, descending, etc."

The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport for the night flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport's operator, Skyport.

Transport Canada was closely monitoring and working with authorities on search and rescue efforts, the country's Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X.

The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and the families of the passengers, Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram.

"We are praying that all six people will be found safe," the statement said.

The US National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information about the situation, but it did not say immediately if it would investigate.

title: How non-monogamy and mental health shaped Rowena Wise's songwriting
text:
Rowena Wise makes music about life's grey areas.

Mixing folksy earnestness with lush indie rock, her songs convey complex subject matter in accessible songs that contemplate "how we put pressure on ourselves to make the right choices, as though there's some moral scoreboard tallying everything up", Wise explains.

" But life is much messier than that … Growth can often come through choices and experiences that don't neatly fit into good or bad. "

Time and again, the Melbourne-based singer-songwriter's second album thrives in contradictions.

The asterisk in the title of new album Bad Things Feel Good* is designed as the "start of an unspoken footnote, implying that not all bad things feel good", Wise tells Double J's Dylan Lewis.

"There's a very long list of exceptions … It allows space for nuance.

Bad Things Feel Good* is the emotive second album from Rowena Wise. (Supplied: Beloved Records)

"I just decided I was in this head space of 'Actually I don't want to tell a clean story about who I am, about morality or love. I'd like to sit in the grey area a bit'. And each song touches on that in a way."

Rejecting simplistic narratives, the album was written while Wise came to terms with "complicated stuff", a messy period involving relationships, mental health and identity crises.

On the ambling title track, she sings of tossing out a faulty moral compass ("the needle's wigging out") in favour of following her heart, her sensitivity underscored by plaintive strumming and sighing pedal steel.

Elsewhere, The Anchor is a tender, spartan tune in which the burden of love feels as crushing as the titular weight.

What ties the album together is that the person in each track, "which is a bit of myself and a bit of others, was standing at the edge of something: of realising, of unbecoming, of transforming".

Blood Ties

Born and raised in Margaret River, Western Australia, Wise grew up part of a family band. Her father, a luthier, hand-made her first instruments.

"I'm so lucky! He's coming up to five decades of making guitars."

Her custom collection includes an acoustic guitar, ukulele, dulcimer and a violin, her primary instrument.

"I like to think my melodies are informed by my background of playing violin," says Wise, who arranged strings for her new album.

At 18, after relocating to Melbourne, she began releasing music under the mononym Ro. Her 2024 debut Senseless Acts of Beauty was shortlisted for the Australian Music Prize, marking her as a keen-edged songwriter. And she's only grown sharper.

She's got a way with setting difficult experiences to music that fans of Julia Jacklin, Stella Donnelly, Carla Geneve and Gena Rose Bruce will recognise and admire.

Having opened for Ball Park Music, Bernard Fanning and Paul Dempsey, Rowena Wise embarks on a headline tour from October. (Supplied: Nick Mckk)

Whether operating in intimate solo mode or fronting a live band, Wise's elegant, drawn-out vocal phrasing makes you lean in and pay attention to her perceptive lyrics.

Inspired by a close friend's heartbreak, Diamond in the Rough reckons with the pressures of maintaining impossible standards.

"I remember watching her still try to be charming and capable around everyone while privately falling apart. She had built so much of her identity around being exceptional, impressive and desirable.

" It made me think about how praise can quietly become a cage. "

Loading Instagram content

The song became about embracing the freedom found in stepping off a perfect pedestal, with strings and slide guitar swelling around Wise as she confides:

"Don't believe what you've been told / You're made of flesh, you're made of blood / You are enough."

The track Blood Ties uses gently distorted guitars to chronicle the experience of another of Wise's friends going through mental illness with their emotionally repressed dad.

"His father loved him, but he didn't quite have the emotional tools to hold space for talking about what was going on.

"He'd grown up in a time where showing vulnerability, especially as a male, was seen as weakness rather than an opportunity to strengthen bonds between loved ones.

"I also saw that my friend had inherited that tendency to just remain silent and hence he didn't reach out enough to his loved ones and family and went through a really hard time."

Loading Instagram content

You wouldn't guess it from the unguarded way she untangles knotty topics, but Wise says she's had "trouble showing vulnerability", having grown up with a "small country town" mentality.

"I think it's so important to be honest with those that you love, otherwise there's this distance that's created. You've got to really open up."

Changing how she saw love

Wise reunited with producer Rob Muinos for Bad Things Feel Good*, recording at his Collingwood studio, The Ratshack.

She spent three days "crammed in a tiny room" knocking out each song with a live band: bassist Rich Bradbeer, drummer Jess Ellwood and Matt Dixon on pedal steel.

"We all together just found a vibe. It was magic."

The ensemble's patient, understated backing adds a rounded, organic quality that accentuates Wise's emotions without overshadowing their intimacy.

A steady rhythm section shepherds the stand-out Unlearning of Love, fuzzy guitars clouding around Wise "coming apart" from an experience with non-monogamy.

It captures the "curious, terrifying but beautiful" tension and thrill of "forming a new connection with someone and not knowing where it sits between platonic and romantic. And wondering if you have to label it at all".

Loading Instagram content

The song feels like a companion piece to last year's No Cure For Love, a moving duet with then-partner and fellow solo artist Didirri (their collaboration dates back to their 2019 song Tea Stains).

Whether scrutinising love or friendships, "unlearning inherited ideas" is a central theme to Bad Things Feel Good*, gifting its songs a sense of uncertainty but also authenticity.

Now in her 30s, Wise believes that, in real life, there is no absolute right or wrong, just "people [who] will try and do their best even if it's not good enough".

Above all else, she still believes in music as "one of the only magic things in the world, because it transcends all sorts of geographic and demographic boundaries".

"It's just got this power of making a whole room of [different] people feel the same thing at the same time.

"And therefore, everyone becomes something beyond themselves. It's as close to spirituality as I think I get."

Rowena Wise's Bad Things Feel Good* tour kicks off at Howler in Melbourne on October 15.

She visits Castlemaine, the Blue Mountains, Sydney, Thirroul, Brisbane and Mapleton, then in November, Hobart and Fremantle.

title: SA government says prior parklands works set precedent for MotoGP circuit
text:
The O-Bahn tunnel and new Women's and Children's Hospital have set precedents for major work in the Adelaide parklands, the state government has argued in a MotoGP circuit assessment.

Mounting a case that the track design will not degrade the national heritage values of the parklands, the government said the area had a long history of accommodating infrastructure works and major events.

It cited the tunnel, new hospital and south parklands stormwater project as examples of works assessed under federal conservation laws and determined not to be "controlled action".

Under those laws, controlled actions are projects classed as having a significant impact on the environment or heritage of a place.

Last week, a Federal Court judge ruled the government's North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment, also on the parklands, did not meet that threshold.

In a separate case lodged recently in the Federal Court, legal action is also brewing against the South Australian government's plans for the MotoGP circuit.

Heritage, flying fox considered

While the MotoGP report acknowledged past projects cannot be used to assess the street circuit, it said they demonstrated that previous "substantial and permanent changes" to the parklands have been judged to have no significant impact on heritage values.

An impression of the SA government's plans for Adelaide's eastern parklands. (Supplied: SA government)

Unlike other parklands projects, it said, the MotoGP circuit mostly involves upgrades to existing infrastructure.

The O-Bahn tunnel opened in 2017 and construction is underway on the Women's and Children's Hospital at the old Thebarton Barracks site.

The arguments relating to the circuit were made in a submission to the federal government as part of a self-referral.

The report also addressed impact on the grey-headed flying fox, a threatened species found in the project area.

It acknowledged that the work would result in a temporary disturbance during construction and when the event is held, and a loss of potential foraging areas.

The grey-headed flying fox at the Botanic Gardens in Adelaide. (Supplied: Brad Leue)

But it said the impacts are localised and there would be no effect on roosting sites or critical habitat.

Overall, the assessment concluded that the MotoGP circuit is unlikely to result in significant impact on the environment or heritage of the parklands.

Public consultation on the submission closed on Friday, with the federal government's assessment now pending.

The report examined the infrastructure, landscape and works associated with the proposed circuit, but it did not look at event operations including the race itself, concerts, spectator facilities and temporary structures.

'Time problem' for government

Revealing the proposed circuit design at the end of August, Premier Peter Malinauskas said the government had received expert advice that a referral to the Commonwealth was not required.

But he said the project would be referred anyway, as a measure to prevent delays.

"We've got a time problem," Mr Malinauskas said.

"We've got to get all this done by November [2027], and so we are naturally concerned about what activist litigation might do if we follow the advice and stick with the self-assessment."

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas made an announcement about Adelaide hosting the Australian MotoGP earlier this year. (ABC News)

Parts of the North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment were stalled during the Federal Court case, which also argued that the project should have been referred.

Dismissing the case on Thursday, Justice Natalie Charlesworth said tree loss and construction on the northern parklands was unlikely to disturb the landscape in a significant way.

title: Regional audiences to lose Network 10, as licensee warns of TV's future
text:
Viewers in parts of regional South Australia, and parts of the Riverina in New South Wales, will lose access to Network 10's terrestrial channels, after the network and license holder, WIN Network, failed to reach an agreement.

WIN has announced it will stop broadcasting 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, with the final broadcasts to be on Friday, October 9.

The network had flagged its agreement with Network 10 would expire in July, and that the channels would be pulled.

However, local audiences were given a three-month reprieve, with Network 10 saying it would provide its feed "free of charge" to WIN while the parties worked on a deal that has not eventuated.

WIN Network says the decision reflects the economics of regional broadcasting. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

High costs of regional TV

In a statement, a WIN Network spokesperson said providing Network 10 services to the impacted markets was "no longer viable".

"This is a business decision that reflects the realities of regional broadcasting," they said.

"Regional markets carry high transmission and infrastructure costs, while digital disruption continues to erode audiences and advertising revenue.

"These economics will continue to make it challenging to maintain services across regional Australia.

"WIN recognises this will be disappointing for viewers and thanks them for their understanding."

The move follows a similar loss of Seven Network channels to the same markets, after Seven and WIN failed to reach an agreement before Seven's deal expired last year.

The channels were eventually restored after a multi-day shutdown that saw the channels replaced with red screens advising they were "no longer available".

Audiences in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith temporarily lost Seven Network channels last year. (ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert)

Country audiences missing out

A Network 10 spokesperson said audiences could continue to access the network's channels online and via its app.

"WIN holds the broadcast licences in the Riverland, Mount Gambier and Griffith regions and although Network 10 has worked closely with WIN to explore options to maintain local access to its content, WIN has advised that continuing to operate them is no longer commercially viable," they said.

" Network 10 remains committed to serving regional Australian audiences. "

The WIN Network holds the broadcast licenses in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith. (ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert)

It is not the first time a regional market has lost Network 10 channels due to the financial challenges of regional broadcasting.

In 2024, audiences in Mildura, Victoria, lost their Network 10 channels when Mildura Digital Television (MDT), which carried 10's signal to the market, was closed by co-owners Seven and WIN.

The networks said "it did not make commercial sense" to keep MDT going, as it had been unprofitable throughout its existence.

A government spokesperson said the decision was a "commercial matter" and that it was up to the networks to explain it to the community.

"The government continues to support Australian broadcasters through a range of measures including the deferral of the Commercial Broadcasting Tax, which will deliver an estimated $111.3 million in savings for the sector," they said.

"We know how important free-to-air TV is and are examining ways to ensure it continues to be delivered in a sustainable way in the future, with public consultation now underway."

title: Treasurer downplays chance of cost-of-living relief amid surging debt
text:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has vowed there will be more savings in the mid-year budget update but downplayed the prospect of more cost-of-living relief for Australians.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had indicated this week help was on the way for households, but Mr Chalmers said the government was looking to run a "tight ship" because of sustained pressure on the budget.

He told Insiders a savings package would feature in the budget update, which is due in mid-December.

"One of the primary influencers on the mid-year update will be the need to find more savings," he said.

"There is very, very substantial and intensifying pressure, not just on our budget but on budgets around the world."

The treasurer said the package would be influenced by the inflation challenge and the "helpful and responsible role" the government "intend to play" to see that figure come down over time.

"So we can get real wages growing again and so some of this pressure can come off people," he said.

Labor defends spending amid high inflation Another interest rate rise has turned attention to domestic pressures contributing to inflation.

On Wednesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to a 15-year high.

Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said she would not "play the blame game", but warned inflation "isn't all about the Middle East conflict".

On Sunday, Mr Chalmers said "no serious observer" would disagree the war in the Middle East was putting "very substantial" pressure on the Australian economy.

He said additional government spending had been concentrated in areas such as bulk billing, to ease pressure on family budgets.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has called for Mr Chalmers to resign. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The Coalition had argued the government was spending too much and had contributed to inflation.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson labelled Mr Chalmers a "disastrous treasurer" and called for him to step down.

"He's actively stoked inflation, and he's fundamentally undermined the success of this country," Mr Wilson said.

Mr Chalmers said the government was not actively considering another discount of the fuel excise discount.

Bond spike to add billions to budget bill

The treasurer also warned the cost of servicing government debt would rise by billions of dollars as borrowing costs around the world increased.

US government bonds were heavily sold off last month, in a sign investors were demanding higher returns to lend money.

Bond market screaming economic trouble ahead Bond yields are the highest they've been in 20 years as inflation fears rip through global financial markets.

Bonds are essentially IOUs issued by governments to borrow money and are bought and sold by large investment funds as well as individual investors.

The bond market is generally seen as safer than the share market, but big swings in bond prices can be an early warning sign of financial stress.

Mr Chalmers said the government's trillion-dollar debt burden would balloon as cheaper debt is paid off, and the government is forced to turn to new, more expensive borrowing options.

"This spike in borrowing costs in the major economies will also play out here," he said.

"The pressure will still come to Australia, unfortunately, and you'll see in the billions of dollars the magnitude of pressure, coming from those bond yields which are changing so quickly."

title: 'Unnecessary and cruel': People with MS to lose home care
text:
Marlene Robinson has been living with the degenerative neurological condition multiple sclerosis for 30 years, with no movement in her legs and limited use of her arms.

The 80-year-old former City of Bayswater councillor and staffer to former Western Australia Premier Geoff Gallop is wheelchair bound and depends on support workers from MSWA for essential personal care, helping her out of bed to shower and dress.

"I can't do that myself, the arms aren't working too well," Ms Robinson said.

Her husband, former anthropologist Michael Robinson, 86, said they could not do without the care.

"It means that just the basic daily needs can be met," he said.

"Whereas if we were just doing it on our own, we probably couldn't do it."

Marlene Robinson and her husband Michael said they depend on support workers for her personal care. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

But the couple recently received a letter from MSWA informing them and 75 other clients that the non-profit organisation would stop providing the Commonwealth-funded Support at Home services.

The program is meant to help older people stay at home instead of moving into residential aged care.

Fears for future

MSWA explained it could not continue because changes to aged care by the Albanese government last year had excessively increased costs and the administrative burden.

The couple received a letter from MSWA saying they are not continuing the Support at Home program. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

It has left Ms Robinson profoundly concerned for her future as she and the other clients, including 16 in the regions, scramble to find a new but inevitably more expensive provider.

She knows other providers' rates are about double MSWA's and she will be able to afford much less care for her basic needs.

"I don't know what I'll do without it," she said.

" When I think about it, I sort of stop. I can't think about the horrific future. "

MSWA was adamant it was not abandoning its clients and would continue providing specialist neurological services.

Chief executive Melanie Kiely said the federal government last year replaced the Home Care Packages program with Support at Home.

Melanie Kiely said it had become unsustainable for MSWA to continue to provide the program. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

"The Support at Home brings in a lot more administration, a lot more regulation into the way we have to do things," she said.

'We understand the pain of this and that is something we want to work with (clients) to transition. Having said that we've kept our prices down so low for so long and we just cannot do it sustainably any longer."

Doubling of rates

MSWA charges $60 an hour for personal care on weekdays, half the market average of $125 an hour.

That means clients face a doubling of the hourly rate.

Marlene Robinson faces the prospect of going into residential care. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

Ms Robinson estimated she would have to pay $1,000 extra from her own pocket to get the same amount of care as before.

"It's a huge amount for us. I mean, we could do it for a month, but you know, we have to survive," Ms Robinson said.

"It just seems so unnecessary and cruel," her husband added.

The couple is now considering whether Ms Robinson can stay at home or will need to go into residential care.

An industry-wide problem

MSWA is proposing to help clients switch to a partner provider.

But this is an industry-wide problem.

MS is on the rise in Australia. Why? The number of people in Australia living with multiple sclerosis has grown by 30 per cent in recent years.

Catherine Stoddart, chair of Advanced Ageing WA and chief executive of Brightwater care, warned higher costs and extra compliance requirements would drive smaller providers under.

"For every hour of care, 31 minutes are spent on administrative work, so therefore people don't get the amount of care that they're entitled to," she said.

"If you're a small provider or have got a small number of clients, that's just too much of a burden to keep going."

Catherine Stoddart said smaller providers may not survive. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

Aged Care Minister Sam Rae's spokesperson said the government's aged care reforms were delivering "stronger provider accountability and enhanced system oversight to support safe, high-quality care".

"We are closely monitoring the rollout of Support at Home to ensure older Australians can access the care they need, when and where they need it, at prices that are reasonable and transparent," the spokesperson said in a statement.

title: A doctor said Tim was incapable of love. His mum knew otherwise
text:
When Judy Sharp was told by doctors that her three-year-old son Tim would be "unfeeling and incapable of love", she refused to accept those limitations.

In the years after his autism diagnosis, Tim began using drawings to communicate with his mum, sharing his feelings, sense of humour and love for her.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

These are Judy and Tim's words.

'What's wrong with your son?'

Judy: When Tim was born in 1988, it was the best day of my life, my heart was ready to burst.

It was the same day the queen was opening the new Parliament House in Canberra, so I thought this is a very special day.

Judy says there were early signs of autism when Tim was just a baby. (Supplied: Judy Sharp)

It wasn't easy after he was born, the first thing I noticed was he didn't sleep.

He was distressed all the time, constant crying and unsettled. As he got older, he had to keep moving, he couldn't stay in the same room as people, and he only ate a few foods.

These were unusual things to me that I didn't understand.

Tim almost looked like he was in pain, you could see the fear in his eyes.

The most common thing that was said to me at the time was, "What's wrong with your son?"

The doctors kept saying, "wait till he's three, to see a specialist".

So, the appointment was made for the day after his third birthday and that was the worst day ever.

Don't tell me that boy doesn't love me

Judy: They sent us to a doctor who was supposed to be the best specialist.

He diagnosed Tim with autism and just wrote him off.

He told me all the things that Tim would never do, that he would be unfeeling and incapable of love.

I had a physical reaction, not only mental and emotional, but it was like someone was sucking the life out of me.

The worst thing anyone can do is take away all your hope and that's what he did.

Judy with Tim and her youngest son Sam (middle). (Supplied: Judy Sharp)

So, by the time I got out of that doctor's office and to the car, I was hysterical.

I'm putting Tim into his little car seat and he's patting me on the back and wiping away my tears.

And I wanted to march back in there and say, "You tell me that boy doesn't love me."

This was perfect love and I knew that little boy loved me.

And I was going to keep on loving him no matter what anyway.

The birth of Laser Beak Man

Judy: One of the things the specialist said to me was that Tim would not speak.

But when he was five, he started to draw.

So, by accident, we started to draw to communicate between the two of us.

And it turned out that Tim had this natural ability for drawing, we thought, "he's got talent".

So, every day, the house was covered in pens, papers, I never put them away.

Tim's Laser Beak Man character has taken him and his mum across the world. (Supplied: Brisbane festival)

Then he did start speaking. And when he was 11, he started walking around the house saying, "When I grew up, I'm going to be Laser Beak Man" — a superhero he had created.

Tim injected his own personality and his own sense of humour into Laser Beak Man.

He's not a classic superhero; he's one defined by Tim in a different way and he's got a very unique way of looking at life.

And Laser Beak Man has taken us on a journey that no-one ever could have imagined; from New York, London, the Sydney Opera House, TV, theatre, movies, you name it.

We've travelled the world with Laser Beak Man and met so many people and Tim's had so many opportunities and things that we never thought would have been possible in any way, shape or form.

Tim: [Drawing] makes me happy and I relax doing it. I can have fun with it. I can use my big imagination.

[Mum and I] made the Laser Beak Man theatre show come true and went to New York with it. He's a superhero and he's really awesome.

One of Tim's drawings of Laser Beak Man represents love. (Supplied: Tim Sharp)

Love is everything, I feel it in everything

Tim: I love that Mum is a good friend and a good mother to me.

She takes care of me.

She is a kind mum.

She sits with me and we don't even talk sometimes, we like being together.

She likes me just the way I am. She makes me feel peaceful and special.

I tell her I love her all the time. I like to help her and make her happy, I like to buy her some flowers and Maltesers.

Love is everything. I feel it in everything. You can see it and hear it. It makes life better and happy.

Tim says love makes "life better and happy". (Supplied: Judy Sharp)

Judy: Tim and I spend most of our time together and I find that a very, very easy thing to do, to be with him.

He's patient and he's kind.

I love that he thinks another way because it makes me think other ways.

I love his natural ability to want to connect with people.

And it's really inspiring to watch him do that in his own way without trying to be like anyone else.

And he will frequently tell me that he loves me.

At the end of the day, he'll say to me, "I've had a really good day with you, Mum. We're a great team."

You don't even get that in a marriage.

The best thing you can do in life is just follow Tim's example; be brave, be yourself and show the world who you really are.

title: 'Forgotten' outback town faces scorching summer without a pool
text:
As the weather turns, residents of inland Australia will begin flocking to their local pool for the start of the swimming season.

But with a scorching summer looming, residents of Walgett in western New South Wales will not be taking part in the seasonal ritual.

The town's pool will remain closed this season after it was deemed unsafe and beyond repair.

Walgett Shire Council says building a new pool is simply beyond the capacity of a small rural council to fund alone. (ABC Western Plains: Emily Middleton)

It leaves few options for cooling off for Walgett parents like Katrina Marshall and her two boys aged 17 and 14.

"Our rivers stink so it's not like the kids can even go down there and enjoy themselves," she said.

" It's going to be a very boring summer. "

Ms Marshall said the closure was a reminder of the disadvantage felt in parts of regional NSW.

"We're always forgotten. We're a little town in the middle of nowhere. We don't exist in Sydney unless kids are stealing cop cars," she said.

Walgett children swimming in the local pool in 2023. (ABC Western Plains: Emily Middleton)

A pool ready to retire

The Walgett Memorial Swimming Pool was first opened to the public in the early 60s.

Sixty years on and the pool is showing its age.

In 2023, council voted to decommission the pool before patching it up to reopen in late 2024.

It closed again in April, before the end of last season, after council deemed it unsafe.

Walgett Shire Council Mayor Jasen Ramien said the council did not want to close the pool this season, but it had no choice.

"The decision to close the Walgett pool was one of the hardest decisions this council has had to make," he said.

" We didn't want to close it, but the reality was the pool had reached a point where it was no longer safe. "

The council will focus on building a replacement pool instead of investing up to $1 million in short-term repairs that were not guaranteed to last, according to a NSW Public Works inspection.

In a letter to NSW Premier Chris Minns, Cr Ramien described the pool as the backbone of the community.

"It is one of the few places in our town that offers relief from the heat, but also relief from boredom, disengagement and isolation," he wrote.

"In a community like ours, that matters more than words can properly capture."

Fixing Australia's aging pools could cost $8 billion. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

The council has requested up to $420,000 from the state government to provide a free daily bus service from Walgett to the Collarenebri Swimming Pool.

The towns are about 75 kilometres apart, with a bus service going once a day in each direction.

Former Olympic swim coach's warning

Former Olympic swim coach Laurie Lawrence is worried the bush faces a generation of kids who cannot swim due to aging pool infrastructure.

"It could be a generation, particularly in the country areas where kids, because they have a lack of pools, don't get to enjoy the water, don't get to stay safe," he said.

"We all deserve an opportunity to learn to swim, the whole country."

Laurie Lawrence says everyone in Australia should have an opportunity to learn to swim. (ABC News: Steve Keen)

Many council-run pools were built in the 60s during the golden era of swimming.

But with a life span of 50 years, most are nearing or have passed their use-by date.

"You can't have the country people being disadvantaged over the city people," Mr Lawrence said.

The National Drowning Report 2026 by Royal Lifesaving Australia found drowning rates were double for those from the most disadvantaged areas and nearly triple for regional residents and nearly quadruple for remote residents compared to major cities.

Walgett Memorial Pool remains closed until funding is found to build a new one. (ABC Western Plains: Zaarkacha Marlan)

The member for Barwon, Roy Butler, has called on the state government to audit pools across the state.

"In New South Wales, 54 per cent of public pools are in regional communities," he said.

"I've spoken to the minister for local government, and the minister for sport about doing an audit of those pools, and I've also taken it up with Royal Life Saving Australia … to get them to pull together a report that prioritises pools so then government can prioritise allocation of funds," he said.

In a written response, a spokesperson for the NSW Minister for Sport Steven Kamper said, "The NSW Government supports sports facilities by providing grant funding and working in partnership with local government, State Sporting Organisations, clubs and associations."

In 2022, the State of Aquatic Facility Infrastructure in Australia report, commissioned by Royal Life Saving Australia, found 500 pools nationally would need replacing, or require "significant repairs" to the pool shell within the next 10 years, at a cost of $8 billion.

Vital blue spaces

Public policy researcher Ian McShane has been following the deterioration and closure of public pools for over 15 years.

He said losing a pool resulted in losing a vital part of a town's social fabric.

"It would be a loss of an important recreational function," said Dr McShane, from the Centre for Urban Research at RMIT, said.

" Local public pools are one place where anybody, regardless of who you are and your social status, can mix. "

Dr McShane said the loss of a pool would mean people might look elsewhere to settle down.

"It can be a tipping point," he said.

"Families would be reluctant to move to areas that don't have good social infrastructure."

Losing a public pool could make people think twice about settling down and raising a family in the area. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Dr McShane said he wants to see pools classed as critical infrastructure, alongside roads and energy networks.

"I think the three levels of government should get together and agree that these are important community places and closing them can really have a significant personal and social impact on communities, particularly small communities."

title: 'Really unfair': Victim-survivor's almost two-year wait for her own records
text:
For years, Sam Morgan kept the memories of the abuse she allegedly experienced while in foster care and at a Tasmanian government school buried.

When she was ready to seek justice, Ms Morgan made a Right to Information (RTI) request to have her foster care and school records, held by the state's education department, sent to her lawyer so she could start a civil court claim against the state.

It took 23 months for the documents to arrive.

"When it drags on for two years … the anxiety just becomes horrific," she said.

Ms Morgan alleges she was physically abused by a foster carer when she was aged 12 or 13, and sexually abused by a foster carer when she was a teenager. She also alleges she was physically abused at a Tasmanian government high school.

The abuse allegedly happened in the 1980s.

Ms Morgan said she was out having a coffee with her daughter when she found out the files had finally been received by her lawyer.

"It was a big surprise but a huge relief. I cried when I got home because it was just a relief," she said.

Her lawyer, Azita Arian, an associate in the abuse law team at Maurice Blackburn, said Ms Morgan was not the only person whose civil court abuse case had been held up because of delays in obtaining records.

"These are people who were abused in state care and they shouldn't have to wait almost two years to access their records," Ms Arian said.

Azita Arian says the RTI delays are limiting the choices victim-survivors have when it comes to pursuing justice. (Supplied: Maurice Blackburn)

She said the records were important because they helped establish when and where people were placed and could help identify foster carers and workers who are relevant to the claim.

She said, in some cases, the files may also document any disclosures of abuse.

Delays reducing choice

Ms Arian said the delays were reducing the choices victim-survivors had when seeking justice.

One of the options they have is the National Redress Scheme (NRS), which does not require the same level of documentation and evidence as a civil court claim, but compensation payments under the scheme are capped at $150,000.

Ms Arian said Ms Morgan had applied to the NRS and was offered a payment of $100,000.

After receiving advice that accepting the payment would essentially bar her from pursuing a civil claim, Ms Morgan has not accepted the offer.

Ms Arian said she had many clients also facing long waits for their records who could not afford to wait.

"Survivors are effectively tunnelled towards redress by default," she said.

Ms Morgan said the delays seemed "to just be really unfair".

"It's almost like the government does it to get people to pull out."

Delays in obtaining her records have delayed Sam Morgan's case against the state of Tasmania. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Ombudsman 'aware of the backlog'

Tasmania's ombudsman has also noted concerns about the delays with RTI applications to the education department.

In an email sent to Ms Morgan's lawyers in May, an officer from Ombudsman Tasmania said their office was "aware of the backlog of requests with the Department for Education, Children and Young People (the department) and concerned by the situation".

"Ombudsman Tasmania staff have been regularly meeting with the department to discuss concerns about the backlog," the officer wrote.

They said the department's "backlog reduction strategies" had "not yet achieved significant progress and the situation is being actively monitored".

The officer also said they were "aware of some applications such as those of your client that have been waiting 18 plus months".

Sam Morgan alleges she was physically abused while a high school student in Tasmania. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Department 'committed to reducing the wait time'

A spokesperson for the Department for Education, Children and Young People said the department was "committed to reducing the wait time to fulfil RTI requests".

"Changes implemented this year, including additional and more senior resources, are expected to further address processing timeframes," they said.

"We will continue to actively engage with applicants or their advocates to identify and prioritise the critical information they need."

Justice Minister Guy Barnett, who has overall responsibility for Tasmania's RTI laws, was also contacted for comment.

Tasmania's child sexual abuse commission of inquiry made recommendations to improve access to records, which are still "in progress" according to the government's latest report on implementation. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

An independent review of Tasmania's Right to Information framework last year found there had been a "rapid growth in volume of applications for access to personal information".

The authors, RTI expert Rick Snell and human rights lawyer Tim McCormack, wrote in their report that they considered the formal RTI application process was "ill-suited for handling requests to access personal information".

They recommended a new system that would protect privacy while letting individuals access their own information.

The Commission of Inquiry into the Tasmanian Government's Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in Institutional Settings also made recommendations aimed at streamlining the process for victim-survivors.

These recommendations were listed as being "in progress" in the government's most recent progress report.

Ms Morgan said she was fortunate to be able to wait the 23 months it took for her records to come through, but it was only the start of the process.

title: Workplace dismissal lawsuit rocks top levels of cancer charity
text:
A research boss at Queensland's peak cancer charity has alleged its chief executive bullied her, and their workplace relationship became so dysfunctional she was told to not contact him directly, according to a lawsuit.

The lawsuit filed by Sandi Hayes, former director of research at the Cancer Council Queensland, marks the latest upheaval for a charity supporting thousands of patients and raising tens of millions of dollars annually.

Cancer Council Queensland is defending the lawsuit and said an investigation found no wrongdoing by chief executive Matt Gardiner. The defence filings allege Dr Hayes had been hostile and disrespectful in a top-level meeting, and was sacked after her and Mr Gardiner's office vibe deteriorated to the point psychological health was at risk.

Cancer Council helps sufferers through counselling, accommodation, a wig-service and research into areas such as early cancer detection. (Supplied)

Started in 1961, the charity helps cancer patients through counselling, accommodation, a wig service and research into areas such as early cancer detection.

It had in 2025 posted a worsening financial situation, high staff turnover and internal gripes.

While latest accounts are yet to be released, the council has now proclaimed financial performance had surged, and it was providing more services and record research investment.

Wrongful dismissal lawsuit

Mr Gardiner declined interview requests but told the ABC in a statement: "Cancer Council Queensland is becoming increasingly effective, increasingly influential and increasingly capable of creating a future where fewer Queenslanders experience cancer."

Mr Gardiner, who started in February last year, also said: "For more than a year, a small group of former employees have pursued a campaign of damaging rumours, misinformation and unsupported allegations."

The Courier-Mail in October last year first detailed a spate of staff departures and concerns, including one employee in a widespread email complaining of a "shift away from emotional, psychosocial and financial support — the very services that have defined [the organisation's] compassion and impact".

Matt Gardiner is the chief executive of Cancer Council Queensland. (Supplied)

The ABC can reveal further upheaval since.

Among that is Dr Hayes claiming she was wrongfully dismissed in an ongoing Federal Circuit Court lawsuit filed against the council, Mr Gardiner and recently appointed chairman Todd Everitt.

Her filings said she had allegedly levelled complaints against Mr Gardiner, including to board members at the Brisbane Club or over a Microsoft Teams chat.

Former Cancer Council Queensland director of research Sandi Hayes. (Supplied)

That included discussing in April last year Mr Gardiner's communication and alleging "integrity and trust issues including equity issues" about his "relationship" with another person at the organisation.

But the joint defence claimed Dr Hayes's concerns then were about the chief executive's work-style and technical understanding of research, and Dr Hayes's gripes were not a complaint under workplace laws.

Both sides' filings detailed versions of clashes such as an argument during budget planning, or about executive titles.

At one stage, Dr Hayes said a staffer sought approval to opt out of a "Pride Month" computer-screen display due to his strong Christian beliefs. Mr Gardiner rejected the request and, according to the defence, said: "Some people will need to think about whether their personal values align with the organisation's values."

Bullying allegations

Dr Hayes's lawsuit also detailed facing several accusations against herself as matters progressed, such as about her conduct at an August meeting with nine organisation executives.

The defence filings alleged an internal investigation determined Dr Hayes had been hostile and disrespectful then, particularly toward the chief executive, while also criticising "two discreet comments" Mr Gardiner had made.

By October last year, Dr Hayes, who at one stage took temporary leave, had alleged bullying and inappropriate behaviour from the chief executive and the other person at the organisation, her lawsuit claimed.

Dr Hayes has taken action in an ongoing Federal Circuit Court lawsuit. (ABC News: Millie Roberts, Patrick Thomas)

That same month, Dr Hayes was told communications between herself and Mr Gardiner must temporarily be emailed via the human resources chief.

The defence filing stated this was based on Dr Hayes's medical advice, Mr Gardiner had received the same instructions and the no-contact directive would uphold both executives' "psychosocial safety".

Court documents also said a commissioned investigation into Mr Gardiner and the other person at the organisation "did not substantiate" allegations raised. Dr Hayes's lawyers could not obtain a copy of it.

Despite mediation attempts, Dr Hayes was ultimately fired this February. The defence filings alleged this was because Dr Hayes could not work with Mr Gardiner without "giving rise to a health and safety risk".

The organisation and Dr Hayes declined to comment on the lawsuit.

Service questions

The spat contrasts with the council's uplifting public presence; its Facebook page profiles people walking or dancing around athletic tracks for its Relay for Life charity event. Volunteers sell yellow daffodils in another fundraising effort.

The organisation told the ABC service levels had risen: providing 26,575 bed nights last year at accommodation centres, up 8.6 per cent, and financial counselling services for 287 people, up 23 per cent.

It added psychological counselling sessions had been decentralised to reach more people.

The charity told the ABC service levels had risen. (ABC News)

The council also said a recent staff engagement result — which consolidates 12 answers — lifted to a "good" 4.1 out of 5.

But one source with knowledge of the organisation said an internal review in February this year indicated staff satisfaction levels had dropped.

That same month, an employee allegedly emailed others describing trying to alleviate pressure on its psychological counselling service, saying some waiting periods were up eight weeks.

The organisation did not dispute either account.

Cancer costs calculated A report investigating the financial and legal impact of cancer in Victoria has found both patients and carers have significant out-of-pocket costs.

At a town hall meeting last December, then chairman Robert Gregg told that meeting the organisation had needed reform. "Things had to change," he said.

He also argued Mr Gardiner had copped blame for changes previously in train. "Matt's a victim of the journey," he said.

The council said staff turnover had been at 42 per cent in the 2025 financial year, improving to 31 per cent last financial year when it employed 185. That is above typical non-profit organisation turnover rates reported by overseas employment and service agencies of between 19 per cent and 21 per cent.

Cancer Council Queensland lost $4.1 million in financial year 2025, with fundraising slightly down while administration, support services and research expenses rose.

The organisation, above a picture of smiling volunteers holding small teddy bears, in August reported its "strongest" operating result in five years. It has not yet released accounts but said last financial year's profit was $3.24 million.

title: Up There Cazaly singer vowed to make AFL grand final after horrific fall
text:
He is a name synonymous with the AFL grand final.

While teams change, pre-game acts change and even the rules themselves change, Mike Brady's performance of unofficial AFL anthem Up There Cazaly has been a fixture of the big day for decades.

Last weekend's grand final was no different — but that was not always a given.

In January, the 78-year-old suffered a horrific fall during a routine evening walk near his Great Ocean Road home.

Mike Brady performed on ABC's Countdown program in 1979 to promote his Up There Cazaly single. (ABC News)

"I fell and landed on my ample backside," he said, laughing.

But the injury was no laughing matter.

Brady described the horror of having to twist his ankle back into place before dragging himself to a nearby fire station, "leaving a trail of blood and mud".

Brady would later learn he had fractured his leg, ankle and foot in 12 places.

With his doctor telling him not to push himself and that it was unlikely he would be able to walk anytime soon, his grand final call-up nine months later was all but certainly out of the picture.

Mike Brady performed before the 2013 AFL grand final between the Hawthorn Hawks and the Fremantle Dockers. (AAP: David Crosling)

When the AFL asked if he would still be up to performing, he vowed to be there even if he had to crawl on stage.

"I said, 'Try and stop me,'" he said.

"Because I love it. It's a part of me."

'The place was closing in on me'

A self-described "outdoors person" who relishes being active, Brady is the first to admit that even he doubted he would make it during parts of the nine-month journey that followed.

"I wasn't doing well," he said.

"I was waking up and felt like the place was closing in on me.

" I was put in a palliative care place, and that was tough because I felt like I shouldn't be there. "

Mike Brady performed during the 2022 AFL grand final match between Geelong and Sydney. (Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

After five months in hospital, he was able to return home with the help of a wheelchair.

He slowly transitioned to crutches, and now mostly gets around using a walking stick.

But Brady defied all expectations and ditched the walking stick to walk out on stage on September 26.

The 100,000-strong crowd gave him the strength not just to walk, he said, but to fly.

"At the beginning of the song, I'm singing it kind of normally, but then I thought, 'I've got this, I'm going to be able to sing it!'

Mike Brady was interviewed about his famed football anthem in 2002. (ABC News)

"I sang harder than I've ever sung before.

"One hundred thousand people reacted, and the roar — I've never heard anything like it.

"It was fantastic. I felt absolutely vindicated for pushing myself so hard."

Musician vows to perform for years to come

Brady says he is not one to dwell on the past and spent much of his recovery writing new poetry and music.

But many hours alone with his thoughts left him to reminisce on a career he never expected.

As an English immigrant, Brady moved to Melbourne at the age of 11.

Mike Brady performed at the 1979 VFL grand final. (Supplied)

The musician and jingle-maker had never even been to a full AFL game when he was asked to create a tune to market the Victorian Football League.

"What an honour," he said.

He went on to pen what would become a footy phenomenon.

Recalling the day he first performed Up There Cazaly at the 1979 VFL grand final, introduced by his friend John Farnham, Brady said it was the first time he felt truly at home in the country he had lived in for nearly two decades.

"I really felt like I belonged in Australia," he said.

"I'd never felt that before. But hearing men and women in the crowd shouting, 'Good on ya, Mike', I really felt the warmth."

Even 48 years later, the feeling remains every time the words "up there Cazaly" leave his mouth.

"I often say the smile on my face when I sing it is actually me chuckling at the irony," he said.

"I love the irony of being a Pommy immigrant that was taken to heart by so many Australian people, and if that's not a great honour, I don't know what is."

Mike Brady says the 1979 VFL grand final, which featured Carlton legend Alex Jesaulenko (pictured), was a key moment in his Up Their Cazaly journey. (Getty Images)

While the honour of performing the track has been handed to other performers over the years, he wants to perform for the next two years, taking it to the song's 50-year anniversary and his own 80th birthday.

"I just hope the crowd is as kind to me as they have been for all those 48 years," he said.

In fact, Brady was more determined than ever to take to the stage this year, fearing the AFL might not ask him back if he did not.

If the crowd's reaction was anything to go by, it was an unlikely fear.

title: Harvest starts on SA crops that 'have not had a setback all season'
text:
The harvesters have started rolling in South Australia for one of the most eagerly anticipated crops in years.

Jesse Chandler was the first to front up to the silos at Thevenard with a load of Commodus barley on September 24.

He farms with his brother Harlee, father Milton and mother Tracey at Charra, halfway between Penong and Ceduna on South Australia's west coast.

Robin Schaefer's wheat ripened well this year. (Supplied: Robin Schaefer)

Milton Chandler said it was the earliest they had ever harvested.

"I think it was 14 or 15 [2014 or 2015] we reaped the Friday before the AFL grand final and delivered on the Monday and this year we reaped on the Thursday so we're a day in front," Mr Chandler said.

"Earliest wheat we put in was on the 8th of April and I was nervous about that, but we've got quite a bit of heavy country and when it gets wet we've just got to go."

Mr Chandler has estimated they would harvest about 4 tonnes to the hectare with their barley.

" Normally even in our good years we'll have a period during the growing season when the crop will have a bit of a moisture check but this year it's almost been textbook. "

"I've been farming here since 1980, and this is the best it's ever looked. It's great, and it's fantastic that it's statewide so it's a real positive for everyone.”

Crop estimate increased

Primary Industries and Regions SA's (PIRSA) crop and pasture report has revised up the state's crop yield forecast again.

The September report found all regions of South Australia had average to above-average winter rainfall with August being the fourth wettest on record.

Disease pressure has increased under the wet conditions with rusts, powdery mildew, net blotch, black leg and sclerotinia reported across several regions.

Overall PIRSA now believes the area sown this year was 4,234,000 hectares and estimates 11,591,000 tonnes will be harvested.

Growers have said they will need every tonne to make up for low grain prices and high input costs.

Robin Schaefer's lentil crop has put on a lot of biomass thanks to early season rainfall. (Supplied: Robin Schaefer)

"We did buy a little bit of diesel through seeding at $3.27; that hurt a little bit, that was a bit of a wake-up call," Mr Chandler said.

"Even though the [grain] prices aren't great hopefully we can [compensate] that with some big yields.

"Logistically it's going to be difficult to deal with it [the size of the crop], but what a great problem."

The September 24 delivery was not the earliest crop that has been harvested in South Australia.

Records show grain has been received as early as September 19 in the past.

Bunge director of industrial management Gavin Cavanagh said the bulk grain handler had been planning for harvest to be two to three weeks earlier than normal.

"We are expecting that we will receive more than we normally would in October given the good start the farmers had and the early plant on the back of those good opening rains," Mr Cavanagh said.

Bunge does a big recruitment drive each year for harvest, putting on an extra 1,500 jobs each year, including overseas workers.

Mr Cavanagh said the changes to visa requirements had not affected its ability to fill roles.

"It hasn't impacted us directly; the majority of travellers we recruit are already in the country.

"From our point of view, we're confident that we've got the right amount of people in the right locations to support our farmers in their delivery pattern."

Perfect timing for storms

With warm, dry weather in SA in recent weeks, the recent storms that delivered about 15 to 40 millimetres of rain across the state were very welcome.

Loxton grain grower Robin Schaefer said he thought he was going to get only a couple of millimetres but ended up tipping 17mm out of the gauge on Friday, October 2.

Robin Schaefer welcomed rainfall across South Australia. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

"It was a lovely surprise," Mr Schaefer said.

"Some of our very early barley is pretty close to going now so that won't benefit, but the majority, I'd say at least two thirds or more of our crop would still benefit".

With so much moisture early in the season the plants have put on a lot of vegetable matter.

" The lentils up here, the biomass is amazing, hopefully that will translate into grain but there's certainly lots of pods on them "

"It does vary a little bit from farm to farm with a number of drought years in a row and the price of fertiliser people couldn't put as much as they would have liked in a year like this to take advantage of it but we're thankful for what we've got.

"It's just wonderful compared to a drought and I think there will be some very tidy yields around right through the Mallee."

Key points A three-bedroom home in Brighton East sold under the hammer for $1,406,000.

In Caulfield South, a four-bedroom property with a pool passed in before selling for $2.6 million.

Two bidders fought it out for a four-bedroom home in Richmond which sold for $1,821,000.

A young family made a single $10,000 bid to buy an Edwardian-style home in Essendon, paying $2.21 million under the hammer on Saturday. The bid knocked out two other parties who had also bid on the four-bedroom home at 11 Wright Street, also young families looking to upsize. The home sold above its $2.1 million reserve and guide of $2 million to $2.2 million. The property sold on the first weekend of auctions since the September interest rate rise, and since new laws were introduced around the disclosure of sale prices, comparable sales and reserve prices. Agents will be required to advertise a vendor’s reserve price at least seven days before an auction is held, albeit a two-week grace period until October 16 meant not all reserves were published this weekend.

Amid pouring rain on Saturday, the Essendon home was one of 714 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. By evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 56 per cent from 506 reported results throughout the week, while 79 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Related Article Interest rates How far house prices have risen since the last time rates were this high Agents said interest rates were top of mind for buyers, with some hoping vendors would drop their price expectations given mortgages would be more expensive, and buyers’ borrowing power would be cut. Selling agent McDonald Upton’s David Mogford said the Essendon auction, held indoors, opened on a vendor bid of $2 million, quickly followed by a $50,000 offer by one of the underbidders. A flurry of mostly $20,000 bids followed until $2.1 million. Offers then dropped to mostly $10,000. The buyers, local to the area, only made the final bid.

Mogford said the property was popular since it had been renovated – though the renovation had been done some time ago. “The vendors have owned the property since 2008 – so 18 years – and it was fully renovated when they bought it. They’ve maintained it really well,” he said. The home was popular because of its renovation. McDonald Upton One underbidder was interested in purchasing prior to auction and had asked about the vendor’s expectations in light of the rate rise, Mogford said. Across the city in Caulfield South, a four-bedroom home at 12 Flowers Street passed in on Sunday morning before selling to a young couple for $2.6 million.

Advertisement

It sold below the $2.7 million reserve, but above the $2.4 million to $2.5 million guide. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Fletchers Bentleigh East’s Tommy Hubert said agents expected two strong bidders, however one of the prospective buyers was advised by a selling agent from another company to not raise their hand. The winners made a $50,000 bid after the auction opened on a vendor bid of $2.4 million. The property, which had a pool, passed in after 10 minutes of silence from the crowd, with the sale negotiated after, Hubert said.

Advertisement

The buyers had help from the bank of mum and dad, he added, and were considering knocking down the home and rebuilding on the 725-square-metre block. Related Article Victoria residential property The Melbourne suburbs where property owners are selling in distress Meanwhile, the party who hadn’t raised their hands had been hoping the home would pass in so they could make an offer. “It’s a good sale all things considered in Caulfield South because similar houses in original condition have been selling for around $2.3 million,” he said. The latest interest rate rise has had an impact, Hubert said, with one potential buyer pulling out as they felt they would be too stretched.

Advertisement

In Brighton East, a three-bedroom art deco home owned by the same vendor for 42 years, sold for $1,406,000 after five bidders competed. The three-bedroom property at 72 Hodder Street sold above its $1.3 million reserve, to a downsizer. Jellis Craig Brighton’s Nick Sinclair said the auction was held under a carport, given the weather. While interest rates weren’t top of mind at the Hodder Street sale, Sinclair said buyers looking for a bargain had been trying to use the rate rise as a bargaining chip elsewhere.

Advertisement

“For those types of buyers it’s the only thing they can really negotiate with,” Sinclair said. “Nine times out of 10, they’re not the best buyer anyway.” Related Article Auctions First home buyers nab architectural Collingwood apartment for $1,106,000 A four-bedroom family home in Richmond sold under the hammer for $1,821,000, above the $1.5 million advertised reserve. The home at 2 O’Connell Street, owned by the same family for 60 years, was snapped up by an investor, one of two bidders. “There were two others [bidders] in the crowd that didn’t get a shot because those two kept going and going,” Biggin Scott’s Andrew Crotty said.

Advertisement

An opening bid of $1.5 million was sought; however, no-one made that offer, with an opening bid of $1.45 million made instead. Offers of $20,000 and $5000 followed, with more erratic $3000, $10,000 or $1000 bids following. Crotty said the interest rate rises were prompting questions from owners wanting to sell. “Vendors are certainly aware of it and are asking how that affects the market,” he said. Buyers and sellers were also aware of changes to reserve price rules. “It doesn’t feel like much has changed,” Crotty said. “It means really having the conversation we’d have on the Thursday or Friday before an auction, a week earlier.”
