title: Elon Musk is back in the White House as privatisation spreads to warfare
text:
Advertisement

WorldNorth AmericaElon Musk Opinion Elon Musk is back in the White House as privatisation spreads to warfare Cory Alpert Former White House staffer October 4, 2026 — 4:30pm

October 4, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Elon Musk is back. Last year, the world’s wealthiest man left the White House after 130 chaotic days as the technically informal head of a department that hacked at the federal government’s ability to deliver on its duties. On his last day, he stood in the Oval Office with a black eye and a golden key to the White House. Weeks later, he ignited a public feud with President Donald Trump, finding himself outside the president’s small decision-making circle. The world’s weathiest man has been appointed to a US committee on the future of warfare. Bloomberg Now Musk has been announced as one of three members of a new Pentagon commission tasked with mapping the future of American warfare, alongside former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, chief executive of military technology company Anduril.

Advertisement

Project Meridian marks a new step in a political transformation larger than any of those men, shifting important responsibility away from democratic government. Rather than privatising how the state operates, Trump’s Washington is now testing the privatisation of decisions about what the state will need. Beginning in 1980, the Reagan administration redrew the line between the private and public sector. Services once seen as the duty of a responsible government were entrusted to the open market, which could price them as they saw fit. Despite the logging of the pillars of government, judgment remained the core responsibility of the state. Companies could sell to the government, but the companies did not decide what a defence strategy required. Project Meridian moves this line yet again.

Advertisement

The old relationship between defence and industry is falling apart. It used to point from requirements, set by the government, to capabilities, built by private companies. Now, the same firms and technologies (including artificial intelligence) cover much more territory on either side of the dividing line between civilian and defence than they did before. A Fury autonomous fighter jet inside Anduril’s California headquarters. Chris Zappone Musk and Luckey lead companies with a combined $US53 billion ($76 billion) in Pentagon contracts and are now tasked with identifying the capabilities that the US military should develop to fight the battles of the future. Luckey described his company’s business model as using “our own money to decide what products to build, how to build then, then we build those products, then we sell them to the government”. He is now one of three people tasked with defining exactly what the government wants to buy.

Advertisement

The neoliberal dream of the 1970s resulted in private companies taking on public tasks. We are now seeing the privatisation of strategic imagination. But governments and businesses are not meant to do the same thing. Navies should not be designed to run a profit. Nor should prisons or hospitals. Governments exist to weigh the interest of its citizens above all else, including alliances and the risk of war itself. This project is part of a longer strategy played out by the Trump administration. In the opening weeks of his second term, Trump signed executive orders making the sale and export of American weapons a top diplomatic and trade priority, to be hawked by American embassies and consulates abroad. The America First Arms Transfer Strategy published this year by the White House says American arms deals are a core part of American foreign policy, used to expand production at home. The administration even made a handy catalogue of items that it encourages allies to acquire, cheapening the highwire task of diplomacy in the 21st century to selling expensive weapons.

Advertisement

The strategy doesn’t stop at bombs. Earlier this year, Trump signed another executive order, declaring another foreign policy goal of the administration to get other countries to adopt American AI technology. Related Article AI Trump rejects AI laws after tech titans agree to ‘self-police’ AI development An ally buying an American F-35 fighter jet is one thing. An ally building its military decision-making capability around American AI models is more tightly wound. As allies become more dependent on American technology, the question of who gets to define the priorities of that technology becomes extremely important. That was made painfully obvious last month with news about OpenAI, a company with deep ties to the White House, gaining unauthorised access to Australian government systems without any human direction.

Advertisement

The stakes for Australia stretch wide. One step below the famous submarines of the AUKUS deal is Pillar II, which focuses on building technological capabilities. It’s designed to make the Australian, British and American militaries work more closely together. The three countries are already jointly testing autonomous systems. They’re sharing sensitive data, and refining how new cutting-edge technology works, together. Integration of the old generation meant ensuring that ammunition from one country could fire in the guns of another. Today, it’s about making sure their software and sensors can talk to each other. A change in how America decides what future military power should look like becomes a change in the assumptions around which Australian defence capability is built. For the past five years, the controversy around AUKUS has been whether it makes Australia too materially dependent on American shipbuilding. The question is now whether Australia is too dependent on American decisions about the future of warfare itself.

Advertisement

The final decisions on how to act and where still reside in Canberra. But the recommendations made by Musk, Luckey and Gingrich will shape the options available. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump is back announcing a 2028 presidential bid. It’s not a joke Cory Alpert Former White House staffer That is, ultimately, why the spectacle of American politics matters so much here, thousands of kilometres away. The decisions made in small rooms in Washington affect how allies, dependent on American systems, can operate. While Reagan’s revolution asked how much the government was needed, this new strategy asks how much decision-making power still belongs to government itself? AUKUS and other alliances mean these questions will not just stay on one side of the Pacific.

Advertisement

Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne looking at the impact of AI on democracy. He previously served the Biden-Harris administration. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

title: WA households are feeling the pinch and making cuts – and one sector will face the most pain
text:
Advertisement

NationalWAAustralian economy WA households are feeling the pinch and making cuts – and one sector will face the most pain Cameron Myles October 4, 2026 — 4:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A new survey has painted a grim picture for Western Australia’s hospitality sector, with households in a glum mood about the rising cost of living and readying to tighten their belts even before the Reserve Bank hiked up interest rates to a 15-year high on Tuesday. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry WA released its September Consumer Confidence survey on Sunday, with almost two in five households surveyed reporting that their expenses outpaced their income each month. WA households are tightening their budgets, and that means cutting back on cappuccinos. Getty Of the 1000 West Australian households surveyed in mid-August, 20 per cent said they had been unable to pay their bills on time, and about half reported they would cut discretionary spending to offset cost-of-living concerns. CCIWA chief economist Dr Daniel Kiely said the hospitality sector would bear the brunt of those discretionary spending cuts.

Advertisement

“Fifty-eight per cent of those surveyed saying they would cut spending on cafes and restaurants over the next six months, which could have a significant impact on the sector heading into the festive period,” he said. Related Article Property prices Why Perth’s housing slump won’t bring relief for everyday buyers “Many consumers have told us they also planned to reduce spending on socialising, with 55 per cent saying they’d spend less at bars, pubs and clubs.” Six in 10 households surveyed reported that interest rates were weighing heavily on their confidence, Kiely said. Their fears were realised on Tuesday, when the RBA board lifted rates to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent.

Advertisement

The move meant a household with a mortgage of $600,000 would be paying another $91 a month, bringing the cumulative increase from the four rate hikes in 2026 to $364. Shadow Treasurer Sandra Brewer said every family across the state had less money than they did five years ago. Speaking to media on Sunday, Brewer took the opportunity to place at least some of the blame at the feet of the Cook government, saying government expenditure was helping drive up inflation. The national consumer price index rose from 3.5 per cent in July to 4 per cent in August, which economists have predicted will keep pressure on the Reserve Bank to push rates higher yet again. Housing costs were the biggest contributor to national annual inflation. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported the cost of new dwellings rose 5.4 per cent in the 12 months to August.

Advertisement

Meanwhile, high global oil prices and the end of the federal fuel excise cut saw transport costs rise 5.6 per cent, which was the second-biggest contributor to inflation. “The best thing government can do is to try and bring inflation down, and that’s by reducing demand in the economy,” Brewer said. “It’s to reduce government spending at a time that the private sector is investing. “So at the moment, last year we had general government expenditure grow by 11 per cent. “In the coming year, it’s forecast to grow at over 8 per cent.

Advertisement

“And we wonder why we can’t get on top of inflation. It’s because Treasurer Rita Saffioti simply won’t pull back. It’s within her power to do so, but she can’t, and she won’t.” Brewer took aim at the government’s “pet projects” – the controversial Burswood racetrack and funding for the Perth Bears NRL team to start up in 2027 among them – and even linked the current inflationary environment to the One Nation byelection shock in Secret Harbour. “People are angry everywhere,” she said. “I think the recent election result in Secret Harbour showed it doesn’t matter what the government says and tells them what a great economy we have, when people are $128 a week worse off for every full-time worker, they know what that means for them and their family.” with Matt Wade

title: Hilary McPhee: The publishing giant who gave rise to Helen Garner, Tim Winton and many more
text:
Advertisement

CultureBooksLiterature Hilary McPhee: The publishing giant who gave rise to Helen Garner, Tim Winton and many more Lauren Ironmonger October 4, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hilary McPhee – a legend of the Australian literary industry who nurtured the careers of writers including Helen Garner and Tim Winton – died on Thursday, aged 85. McPhee Gribble, the publishing house she founded with Diana Gribble in 1975, shaped a generation of iconic Australian writers – among them Kathy Lette, Dorothy Hewett, Kaz Cooke, Drusilla Modjeska, Jennifer Dabbs and John Misto. Their slate of influential novels includes Winton’s Cloudstreet, Garner’s Monkey Grip and Lette and Gabrielle Carey’s Puberty Blues. Writer and editor Hilary McPhee founded McPhee Gribble Publishers with Diana Gribble in 1975. “I published my first four books with McPhee Gribble. Hilary was a fine editor. I’ll always be grateful for that,” says Garner. Winton was just 24 when he first walked into the McPhee Gribble offices, housed in a converted factory in Melbourne’s Fitzroy. The young novelist had come to the publishers by way of literary agent Caroline Lurie, after his first publishers Allen & Unwin didn’t want him to write a collection of short stories.

Advertisement

“I was excited and daunted,” says Winton of their first meeting. He was already aware of McPhee’s prowess as the publisher of Monkey Grip. Editor's pick Review How two women changed the patriarchal world of Australian publishing With Winton working from Western Australia, much of their decades-long partnership unfolded through letters. The pair were corresponding until not long before her death, reminiscing about their time together. “Her handwriting is very familiar to me, it was always pencil on the page, and she was a sensitive and canny editor. She knew when to push, and she was someone you could trust,” says Winton. He recalls McPhee showing up unexpectedly at a reading of his in 2024 for his novel Juice.

Advertisement

“She didn’t have any airs and graces, you know, there was the great Hilary McPhee waiting for it to be signed. And she wrote to me afterwards saying how proud she was and how pleased she was to be there.” Tim Winton pictured in 1984, the year he first won the Miles Franklin award. Together, McPhee and Gribble were trailblazers in the old boys club of Australian publishing. As McPhee wrote in her 2019 memoir Other People’s Words: “The strong men in publishing liked to call in the late afternoons with bottles of wine and kindly advice: stick to packaging, do horse books or ballet books … put together some recipes … get a good-looking, famous sheila to front them for you …” Nikki Christer, a publisher who inherited Picador from McPhee (and its writers such as Winton, Lily Brett and Kate Grenville), describes her predecessor and mentor as a “curious”, “loyal” and “incredibly generous” editor with a “deep respect for the writer’s voice”. “She was part of a generation that transformed Australian publishing. When she and Di created McPhee Gribble, it was largely dominated by overseas publishers and imported books. And so she helped create a publishing culture that put Australian writers and therefore Australian stories at the centre,” she says.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Literature 'The solitude was terrifying': Hilary McPhee on learning to be alone In 2001, Christer published McPhee’s first memoir, Other People’s Words. “It was a really interesting experience to be on the other side of the great editor who then became the writer. She had her own ideas about it … I did find I was slightly intimidated by her as I think we all were. Not that she made you intimidated, she just was a grand figure of Australian publishing,” Christer recalls. “She had that way of looking at you where she would close her eyes and lift her chin, and you would know that you’d said something stupid. She didn’t suffer fools.” McPhee is survived by three children – Sara, Rupert and John. Her business partner and friend, Diana Gribble, died in 2011.

Advertisement

Born in Melbourne in 1941, McPhee’s first foray into the world of publishing was as an editorial assistant at literary journal Meanjin, while studying history and literature at The University of Melbourne. During these student years, she cultivated wide interests, including launching a small magazine, Theatre, and embarking on archaeological expeditions. In 1964 – her final year at university – McPhee married artist Peter Freeman, with whom she would have two children. The pair travelled around Europe and the Middle East before settling in London for a time where McPhee worked at the British Council compiling exhibition books. McPhee in 2001. Craig Abraham

Advertisement

Returning to Australia in 1969, McPhee worked at Penguin Australia, then McKinsey management consulting firm as their first female writer, before starting her own publishing house with Gribble, whom she had met through the women’s movement. Both young mothers, their Fitzroy offices had a crèche, unusual for the time. “When they got too adventurous – climbing out windows and appearing naked on the first floor, escaping from their childminder – they were sent to childcare very quickly. But for quite a while, we did have children in the office, and it was wonderful having them there. We had a nursery that they slept in and a marvellous woman who’d raised six children looking after them,” McPhee told Kill Your Darlings earlier this year. A licensing arrangement with Penguin, publishing the hit children’s book series Practical Puffins (which went on to sell three million copies worldwide), helped keep them afloat in their early years as they set about platforming young Australian voices. The pair published hundreds of titles under their imprint, including those of young Indigenous authors, and fostering the fledgling careers of editors and publishers like Sophie Cunningham and Sue Hines.

Advertisement

Speaking to this masthead in 2022, 46 years after a then unknown Helen Garner walked into their offices, McPhee said: Editor's pick Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos. Literature ‘A poet in plain prose’: Reflections on Helen Garner’s amazing opus “Helen arrived one day on her bicycle with two copies of the manuscript of Monkey Grip in green foolscap folders. This is what writers did in those days, you gave publishers two copies. Di and I each took a manuscript home, read it overnight and rushed in the next day and said we’ve got to publish it.” In 1979, McPhee, Gribble, Joyce Nicholson, Anne O’Donovan and Sally Milner founded Sisters Publishing, a mail order feminist book club that published poetry and fiction “by women, for women”. But by the 1980s, recession hit the Australian publishing industry and the pair signed a co-publishing deal with Penguin before selling McPhee Gribble entirely to Penguin in 1989.

Advertisement

McPhee stayed on for a few years before moving to Pan Macmillan, where she ran the Picador imprint until 1994 when she was headhunted by then prime minister Paul Keating to become the first female chair of the Australian Arts Council. There, she played an instrumental role during a turbulent time for the council – leading a controversial restructuring under Keating. After John Howard was elected prime minister in 1996, he attempted to shut the council down, a feat which McPhee later said embarrassed her terribly when she received an Order of Australia for her services to literature in 2003. As well as penning two memoirs, McPhee published Wordlines (2010), a selection of contemporary Australian writing, and an annotated edition of filmmaker Tim Burstall’s 1950s diaries, Memoirs of a Young Bastard. In 1998, she received an honorary doctorate of letters from Monash University. She served on the judging panel of prestigious awards including the Miles Franklin Literary Award, the Victorian Premiers Award and the Melbourne Prize, and was director and acting editor for a time of online political journal New Matilda.

Advertisement

In 2006, fleeing a failed marriage, McPhee moved halfway around the world, chasing a writing project in the Middle East and immersing herself in the lives of other, solo-living women in Italy and England. She detailed the terrifying solitude of this time in her memoir Other People’s Homes. The Australian publishing industry may not look quite the same as it did in 1976, when McPhee entered the scene, but it’s no doubt all the better thanks to her sharp eye and fierce belief in the people who make it what it is. Her enormous legacy lives on in the pages of Cloudstreet, The Children’s Bach (McPhee’s favourite of Garner’s works) and countless others. title: This 345-kilometre undersea power cable will power Victoria but may ruin dairy farmers
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaRenewables This 345-kilometre undersea power cable will power Victoria but may ruin dairy farmers Benjamin Preiss October 4, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To the untrained eye, the disruption to Paul Peluso’s property from a major interstate electricity transmission line seems minor, perhaps even lucrative. Peluso’s dairy farm lies in the proposed path of the Marinus Link project, which includes 345 kilometres of power and data cables running from north-west Tasmania to the Latrobe Valley in Victoria. The cables will run beneath the Bass Strait and continue underground in Victoria. Whether they want to or not, many Victorian landholders including Peluso will host them. Paul Peluso on his dairy farm. Joe Armao It is crucial national infrastructure for electricity sharing between states, its backers say. But Peluso fears the four-hectare easement on his 180-hectare farm will ruin his dairy business in Mirboo North.

Advertisement

“What they’re proposing to do will shut me down as a dairy farmer,” he said. Marinus Link will dig a trench for the cables and has a six-year window to access his land. Peluso said this would cut across tracks his cows used to move between paddocks and milking sheds. “These main tracks are the arteries that pump the animals to where they need to be.” The vessel, Leonardo da Vinci, will be used to lay the Marinus Link electricity cable between Tasmania and Victoria. Peluso said Marinus Link had made an initial compensation offer during the construction period, in addition to $8000 per kilometre annually on his property for 25 years.

Advertisement

Peluso declined to disclose the construction payment offer, but he said it paled into insignificance against the losses he expected to incur. He is not alone. Many farmers have raised concerns about Marinus Link’s impact on their operations. Peluso’s niece and former Victorian Farmers Federation president, Emma Germano, said real estate agents had advised there would be little interest from buyers in her uncle’s farm while there was uncertainty about the construction works and easement. Emma Germano and her uncle, Paul Peluso, with dog Bonnie, are worried about Marinus Link’s impact on his farm. Joe Armao Germano, who is helping Peluso negotiate fair compensation, said the plans would hurt the farm’s value.

Advertisement

“Why would you buy this dairy farm when you can buy somewhere else with no easement and no construction?” she said. The easement crosses where Peluso loads cattle, but Germano said Marinus Link had rejected a request to move it to a back fence to minimise disruption. Although the cables will be buried, Germano said water movement on the property would be permanently altered and soil disturbances could hamper grass growth. She said there was a power imbalance, making it difficult for farmers to engage in fair compensation negotiations with a big company. The underground cables will run through Paul Peluso’s property. Joe Armao A Marinus Link spokesman said it had engaged with landholders since 2019, including discussions about the route through their land, and was committed to respectful negotiations. He said the company would resort to compulsory acquisition only when absolutely necessary.

Advertisement

The spokesman said the length of time the company needed on each parcel of land depended on many factors from weather to geotechnical conditions. “The best thing we can do is have really open discussions with each landholder on what this will mean for them,” he said. The spokesman said land access involved more than construction and was required for engineering and technical design surveys, and environmental and cultural heritage considerations. An image of a Hitachi valve hall at a converter station in Europe. Marinus Link will consist of two Hitachi valve halls in Tasmania and Victoria to house the electronics that will convert alternating current to direct current and vice versa. In addition to power and fibre-optic cables, Marinus Link will include a communications station and converter stations on both sides of the Bass Strait.

Advertisement

It has attracted less controversy than above-ground projects VNI West and Western Renewables Link, where communities have railed against soaring towers. Related Article Renewables The 345km undersea cable that will help Australia move on from coal The Victorian government approved the environmental effects statement for Western Renewables Link, but Premier Ben Carroll ordered a cost review, raising questions about its future. The Marinus Link cables will run 255 kilometres undersea in Bass Strait and 90 kilometres underground in Gippsland, crossing the shore at Waratah Bay and then on to Latrobe Valley. The federal, Victorian and Tasmanian governments are partners in the venture. The first stage of Marinus Link will have 750-megawatt capacity – enough to power about 750,000 homes.

Advertisement

Tasmania can generate power with its hydroelectric dams, allowing power to flow to Victoria when needed. Likewise, Victoria often produces excess electricity from solar and wind farms during the day, which could go to Tasmania. Related Article Energy Power struggle: Coalition pledge to scrap towers sparks bill warning The first stage is due for completion in 2030 and the second in 2033. In August last year, the Australian Energy Market Operator confirmed the project would cost about $7.57 billion for stages 1 and 2. Preparatory works have already begun at Sandy Point. Construction will involve a method known as horizontal directional drilling to install cable conduits under the beach at Waratah Bay. Nexa Advisory chief executive Stephanie Bashir said Marinus Link would form a crucial part of Australia’s energy infrastructure with enduring benefits and was worth the cost.

Advertisement

She said neither Victoria nor Tasmania could rely solely on the electricity they produced alone. While Victoria is currently a net exporter of electricity, Bashir said, the closure of coal-fired power stations from 2028 would result in Victoria needing to import electricity. “Our modelling shows that every year of delay, our bills go up,” she said. Nexa forecast average Victorian wholesale prices could increase up to 37 per cent between 2027 and 2031. Bashir said delaying projects like Marinus Link could cost Victorian households up to $472 over those four years. Grattan Institute energy and climate change deputy program director, Hamish McKenzie, said Marinus Link should theoretically keep power prices down in each state. More electric vehicles, data centres and households switching to electric appliances and heating are expected to drive up demand for power in coming years.

Advertisement

The closure of the Yallourn power station in 2028 is another factor set to reshape Victoria’s energy system. “We don’t have enough renewable generation to replace that,” McKenzie said. He said new transmission infrastructure would become increasingly important to meet Victoria’s electricity requirements. “If VNI West doesn’t proceed then Marinus Link becomes even more important,” McKenzie said.

Advertisement

Green Energy Markets chief executive Tristan Edis said Marinus Link was initially based on the idea that Tasmania would become the battery of the nation, but battery technology was now rolling out across Australia. “I do think we haven’t thoroughly evaluated other ways to solve those problems,” he said. Marinus Link has discussed with community groups local causes it can support. Among them is South Gippsland Landcare Network, which is seeking support to rehabilitate the Tarwin River catchment. Paul Peluso on one of his farm tracks. Joe Armao

Advertisement

Network chair Jillian Staton said Marinus Link should back local community and sport groups as part of its social licence, but Marinus Link should also leave a lasting environmental benefit. “Footy shirts are great, but this [Tarwin River] project is an opportunity for Marinus to have a positive long-term impact on the whole community,” she said. title: Buckley pulls out of North coach race as Lions board considers selection process
text:

Nathan Buckley has withdrawn from the race to become North Melbourne’s next senior coach, delivering a major twist in the Kangaroos’ search for Alastair Clarkson’s replacement. Two industry sources who spoke on the condition of anonymity confirmed to this masthead that Buckley had informed those involved in the process that he will not pursue the vacant position, ruling himself out of a return to senior coaching at Arden Street. Nathan Buckley splits his time as a Geelong assistant coach and Fox Footy analyst. AFL Photos Buckley was due to formally present to the coaching panel on Saturday, but told the club late last week that he would be removing himself from the process. It means Clarkson’s successor is set to be a first-time coach, with Daniel Giansiracusa, Jaymie Graham, David Hale and North assistant Xavier Clarke all in the mix.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘One of the hardest things I’ve done’: Three-time premiership coach Chris Fagan retires a Lions legend The Roos’ hunt for a new coach coincides with Brisbane’s, who need to replace retiring triple-premiership coach Chris Fagan. The Lions board will meet this week to decide whether to conduct a targeted process or throw the vacancy open to all candidates. Buckley had loomed as one of the most compelling candidates available to North as the club searches for the coach to lead its next era. His decision leaves the Kangaroos without one of the biggest names in the market and will force them to narrow their focus elsewhere as they continue the process of appointing Clarkson’s successor.

Advertisement

Buckley, 54, coached Collingwood for almost a decade, taking the club to the 2018 grand final and within a kick of a premiership, before stepping away in 2021 after 218 games in charge. He has since rebuilt his football profile through the media and repeatedly resisted opportunities to get back into the coaches’ box before joining the Cats as an assistant coach in 2026. Viney and club president Sonja Hood didn’t shy away from being frank about why they had sacked Clarkson Ruby Alexander The Kangaroos are searching for another coach after parting ways with Clarkson following four seasons in which the four-time premiership coach managed just 20 wins from 81 games. President Sonja Hood raised eyebrows in the media conference announcing Clarkson’s sacking by stating North needed a coach for the modern game.

Advertisement

North believed their young list had reached a point where it required a different voice and a coach suited to taking the group through the next phase of its development. Having already made the enormous call to move on from Clarkson, and having accumulated elite young talent through the draft, the Kangaroos are under pressure to get their next appointment right. Related Article Analysis

Trading and drafting On the market: Your team by team guide to AFL trade period The Kangaroos last week appointed three-time premiership Tiger Kane Lambert as head of development. Buckley’s decision to walk away from the North Melbourne opportunity after missing out on the top job with incoming side Tasmania suggests he is prepared to wait for the right job before returning as a senior coach.

Advertisement

He will continue as Chris Scott’s assistant at Geelong into 2027. North Melbourne and Buckley were contacted for comment. At Brisbane, the Lions have several strong internal candidates to consider as potential replacements for Fagan, who led the team to their third consecutive flag when they defeated Fremantle in the grand final. Brisbane Lions football manager Danny Daly is likely to be a candidate for the Lions’ vacant coaching position. AAP His long-time lieutenant Danny Daly is at the front of the queue, while assistant coach Cam Bruce is also a potential candidate, though the board will discuss which approach it takes to replace Fagan.

Advertisement

Bruce did his apprenticeship at the Hawks before becoming highly regarded at the Lions. Daly, who would need to be replaced as football manager if he were to take over from Fagan, started as an assistant coach at North Melbourne in 2003. He spent time at Richmond before joining the Lions in 2015, two seasons before Fagan’s appointment. He became football manager in 2021 but was Fagan’s eyes and ears in the coaches box on match day and indicated on SEN before last week’s grand final he had a desire to be a senior coach. Brisbane coach Chris Fagan is going out on a high with the club facing an unprecedented decision to replace him. AFL Photos via Getty Images “I’m not sure what life would be like without ‘Fages’ there so we might have to decide a few things myself. At the end of the day, it’s what’s best for the football club – whether that’s myself or a Cam Bruce, Dale Morris or getting someone new in,” Daly said. “That will be their decision and I’m happy with whatever they decide.”

Advertisement

Although Fagan had informed some key confidantes this would be his final season, the board had not been in a position to discuss a potential successor until the decision was official. Despite his success, Fagan was not among the highest-paid coaches in the game during his tenure, which enabled the Lions to fully resource the football department within the soft cap. It makes attracting an experienced coach – such as Adam Simpson and Buckley – or attempting to poach a current coach – such as former Lions premiership players Chris Scott (Geelong) or Craig McRae (Collingwood) – more unlikely than likely. The board could decide to look at a field of first-time coaches, which may include former Lion Murray Davis who is now at the Crows. Davis was interviewed for the Essendon coaching job won by Mark McVeigh. The Lions have not contacted external candidates directly.

Advertisement

Adelaide’s Matthew Nicks, St Kilda’s Ross Lyon, the Western Bulldogs’ Luke Beveridge and the Eagles’ Andrew McQualter are out of contract at the end of 2027. McQualter is a chance to have his contract extended before the start of next season. Only six coaches before Fagan have coached their team to a flag and not coached them the next season. Hawthorn’s Allan Jeans was the most recent, when the legendary coach handed over the reins to Alan Joyce for a season in 1989 due to ill health. The Hawks went back-to-back. Alex Jesaulenko left Carlton at the end of 1979 after a board upheaval and was replaced by Peter “Percy” Jones, while John Kennedy vacated the Hawks job in 1977 and handed it over to David Parkin on the eve of the 1978 season for family reasons. Neither team won the flag the next season.

Advertisement

Frank “Checker” Hughes was replaced at Melbourne by Allan La Fontaine in 1949 after a long coaching career at Richmond and Melbourne. Reg Hickey replaced Charlie Clymo after Clymo coached for one season for one premiership in 1931 while Charlie Ricketts vacated the post at South Melbourne after winning the 1909 flag. Lions CEO Sam Graham said on Thursday the club would announce its “next steps to appoint our next senior coach in due course”. The Lions retained their key players Logan Morris and Zac Bailey beyond this season. Lachie Neale has joined Collingwood as an unrestricted free agent while Sam Marshall has nominated St Kilda as his preferred destination. title: The private paradise of crypto’s most powerful ex-convict
text:

Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates – One morning in June, cryptocurrency mogul Changpeng Zhao pulled up to the St. Regis resort in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in a Nissan SUV. Zhao is the richest man in crypto, worth an estimated $US114 billion ($164 billion), and he lives in a villa nearby, with nine bedrooms, four bodyguards, a chef and a yacht. But he also likes to play the part of a “normal dude”, as he often describes himself, and that day he had offered to give me a personal tour of the city. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao was pardoned by US President Donald Trump last year after pleading guilty in 2023 to federal charges relating to violations of the American Bank Secrecy Act. Bloomberg Zhao, to be clear, isn’t a normal dude. Not long ago, US authorities brought a criminal case against him for his management of Binance, a crypto exchange depicted in court papers as a haven for Russian money launderers, Iranian sanctions evaders and Islamic State terrorists. Zhao pleaded guilty and escaped with his fortune intact. After serving a four-month prison sentence, he returned to Abu Dhabi, still Binance’s majority shareholder and still the most powerful figure in the industry. These days, Zhao, 49, moves through the world like a head of state, flying around Asia on his private jet to advise governments on crypto regulation. Zhao’s most influential allies are a pair of powerful ruling families. One is the clan that runs the UAE, which wants his help creating a technology powerhouse in the desert. The other is the Trumps.

Advertisement

Last year, Binance forged a business relationship with World Liberty Financial, the crypto start-up founded by US President Donald Trump and his three sons. World Liberty generated $US799 million for Trump last year — his single most lucrative asset. Trump pardoned Zhao last October, a move widely criticised as a quid pro quo. Known in the industry as “CZ”, Zhao often avoids reporters, but he met me several times this year, eager to put a friendlier gloss on his career at Binance, which still hasn’t stanched the flow of dirty money. For years, his true calling has been what academics term “jurisdictional arbitrage” — moving from country to country in search of a legal framework pliable enough to accommodate his appetite for risk and growth. In Abu Dhabi, he may have found an ideal base of operations. As we drove into the city, we passed a string of impressive compounds and drove towards the presidential palace, Qasr Al Watan, whose striking white dome resembles the Taj Mahal. Zhao was growing animated. “Democracy has been hailed as, like, the holy grail for the last couple hundred years, but democracies are inefficient,” he said. “If you get a benevolent dictator, it’s actually extremely efficient. There’s very little debate going on. You don’t waste time on a lot of frivolous stuff.” Related Article Analysis

US midterm elections America’s billionaires are turning their backs on Trump Lately, this top-down model of business and politics, simultaneously medieval and ultramodern, has gained traction in the United States. On a trip to Abu Dhabi last year, Trump called the nation’s ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, “a very strong man” and “a man of vision like few others”. Zach Witkoff, the son of one of Trump’s top advisers, put it more bluntly at a crypto conference in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, in May 2025. “We really need to take a page out of His Highness’ and the Emirates’ book,” Witkoff said. “They are just an amazing example of how you can lead with innovation while also maintaining your family values.”

Advertisement

One day early this year, Zhao was working when the windows began to shake. He got up and walked onto his balcony, where he saw a trail of smoke in the sky. Zhao lives on Saadiyat Island, an enclave of Abu Dhabi across the Persian Gulf from Iran, which had just fired a missile at the UAE. It was the start of a geopolitical crisis that has destabilised the region, but Zhao was not overly concerned. He returned to work. Billionaires gravitate to the UAE for billionaire reasons. The country doesn’t levy an income tax, and it’s considered extremely safe. Getty Images Until he settled in the UAE, Zhao was a man without a country. He was born in China, then moved to Canada with his family at the age of 12. After attending McGill University, he worked a series of technology jobs. In July 2013, over a poker game in Shanghai, a colleague suggested he check out “this new thing called bitcoin”. After a few months of study, Zhao made a radical bet. He sold the family home — a three-bedroom apartment in Shanghai where he and his wife were raising two children — and ploughed the $US900,000 in proceeds into bitcoin. Zhao went on to work at a succession of crypto start-ups in Asia. In July 2017, Zhao founded Binance. Within a few months, it was the largest exchange in the world, a title it has never relinquished. Binance’s success rested on two pivotal insights. The first was that crypto investors were drunk on risk and would never be satisfied swapping dollars or yen merely for an equivalent amount of crypto. For years, Binance has operated as a margin exchange: Traders can borrow money to place high-risk, high-reward bets on the prices of bitcoin and other popular tokens.

Advertisement

The second insight was simpler yet more consequential. Many crypto investors didn’t want to identify themselves, and Binance didn’t ask them to. For its first four years, the company allowed customers to open accounts without providing even the most basic KYC — the “know your customer” information that traditional companies require to prevent financial crime. The result was an extremely lucrative free-for-all: a platform where unvetted investment products were available to unvetted traders. As the market boomed, Binance took a cut of each transaction; the company quickly reached $US1 billion in profits, according to Zhao’s self-published memoir, Freedom of Money. Zhao was suddenly a crypto celebrity. But he has never been widely understood outside the industry. When he recounts his most contentious moments, Zhao portrays himself as a kind of passenger — a crypto nerd overwhelmed by success, a naive outsider. Related Article Billionaires Billionaire pardoned by Trump is back in the spotlight It is not always a convincing performance. In June, Zhao told me that he had “never really wanted” to break the law in Binance’s explosive early years, when the company’s lax controls allowed a procession of bad actors to launder money. “It’s just my lack of experience in that area,” he said. That image isn’t compatible with the evidence US prosecutors collected in their investigation into Binance. In court, they quoted an admonition that Zhao had given his underlings: “Better to ask for forgiveness than permission.” Privately, Zhao had discussed ways to obfuscate that Binance served American users even though it wasn’t licensed in the US, according to legal filings. “Don’t leave anything in writing,” he told a subordinate. Royal treatment

Advertisement

Zhao paid a visit to the UAE in 2021, after years of roaming around Asia. In 2017, he and his Binance colleagues had been forced to flee China, as the government prepared to announce a ban on crypto exchanges. A stint in Japan hadn’t worked out either, nor had Singapore. Then Zhao’s friend, Gabriel Abed, a businessperson who served as the ambassador to the UAE for Barbados, made a suggestion. He told Zhao to check out Dubai. Immediately, Zhao saw how the UAE treated the rich and powerful. He arrived in Dubai on a Saturday morning in October, and within hours, a government minister, Omar Sultan al-Olama, came to visit. He offered Zhao a so-called golden visa, which grants 10 years of hassle-free residency. A doctor was summoned to conduct the blood test required of all visa holders. Applications often take weeks to process; Zhao was approved in less than 12 hours. Not everyone in the UAE is treated so generously. Over the years, the nation’s leaders have conducted mass surveillance, outlawed even the mildest forms of dissent, and overseen a labor market where foreign workers are frequently exploited and abused. But for Zhao, it was the beginning of a comfortable new life. Before founding Binance, he had separated from his wife, who moved to Tokyo with their children. He started a relationship with one of his colleagues, He Yi, a marketing executive. While his older children attended college in the US, Zhao and He raised a young family in the UAE. Zhao got to know a group of Emirati leaders who were curious about technology. Eventually, he worked his way up to the brother of Sheikh Mohammed, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. During these early encounters, the sheikhs would pitch Zhao on the UAE, asking what they could do to help him. Soon, Zhao was preaching the nation’s virtues to the broader billionaire community. He encouraged artificial intelligence mogul Sam Altman to set up a corporate presence in the UAE, warning that other countries would treat him with hostility. UAE’s National Security Adviser Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan is a big backer of crypto. AP

title: On the market: Your team by team guide to AFL trade period
text:

The AFL trade period officially opens on Monday when the list managers from all the clubs gather at Marvel Stadium to get serious about the deals that will shape their teams for 2027. In truth, negotiations have been bubbling along for months for some players. The big questions are: Will Zach Merrett make it to Hawthorn at his second attempt? Will Gold Coast match Hawthorn’s free agency offer for Ben King and thereby force a trade? Where will Melbourne heart and soul player Jack Viney land? We examine every club and which players are on the market. Jesse Hogan, Rowan Marshall, Zach Merrett and Jack Viney are likely to feature in the trade period. Marija Ercegovac/Getty Images Follow our live blog every weekday during the trade period, which closes at 7.30pm on Wednesday, October 14. Adelaide

Draft picks: 13, 32, 33, 41, 54, 90

Key players: Nick Murray, Luke Pedlar The Crows were in the box seat for Zac Bailey, only for Bailey to remain a Lion on an eight-year deal. The Crows are set to lose Pedlar to Port Adelaide, but have a call to make on whether they trade key defender Murray, who has a five-year offer from North Melbourne. Murray, who has managed 78 games in six seasons with the Crows, including 11 this year, is contracted for another two seasons. Fellow tall backman Jordon Butts has already left for the Bulldogs in free agency. The Crows have been linked to Suns defender Charlie Ballard. Bigger picture, they are expected to make a play for St Kilda’s Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera and Hawthorn’s Will Day next year. - Jon Pierik Brisbane Lions Draft picks: 18, 39, 40, 51, 57, 77, 95

Key players: Keidean Coleman, Will McLachlan, Sam Marshall The Lions are likely to lose Marshall, who has requested a trade to St Kilda, while forward McLachlan has been linked with Essendon and Melbourne. Lachie Neale is off to Collingwood as a free agent, but Brisbane received only pick 39 as compensation, which will not help them match a bid on potential top-10 academy selection Caylen Murray. Out-of-favour defender Coleman is open to a fresh start at a different club. - Marc McGowan

Moving on: Star midfielder Lachie Neale has had a week of partying after the AFL grand final, but will soon be on his way to Collingwood. Getty Images Carlton Draft picks: 11, 16, 23, 24, 59, 70, 88 Key players: Hudson O’Keeffe, Flynn Riley The Blues have locked in ex-Swans key forward Joel Amartey through free agency, and their primary draft focus is matching a bid on Cody Walker, the son of former Blue Andrew Walker. Their top two selections in the draft add up to 2396 value index points, and they can also go into draft deficit, meaning they will have enough points to cover a bid up to No.2. Carlton also hope to land Giant Lachie Whitfield, while ex-Magpie Wil Parker will join as a delisted free agent. Ruckman O’Keeffe has requested a trade to the Western Bulldogs, while Riley is keen to move to the Magpies on a three-year deal. - Jon Pierik

Collingwood Draft picks: 9, 28, 66, 68, 75, 86

Key players: Scott Pendlebury, Dan Houston, Jordan De Goey, Harry DeMattia The Magpies are determined to remain in the premiership mix, and have landed three-time Brisbane premiership star Lachie Neale, who proved through a tumultuous 2026 campaign that his on-field output won’t be impacted by off-field headlines. A fourth-round pick will be enough to secure Giants forward Jesse Hogan, while they have met with Richmond’s rebounding defender Jayden Short. List boss Justin Leppitsch confirmed the Magpies were open to trading Jordan De Goey, who has a year left on his contract, but wants a long-term deal. Dan Houston’s future remains a point of interest, although he is contracted until the end of 2030 and his management has declared he is going nowhere. Scott Pendlebury will cross to Gold Coast. - Jon Pierik New colours: Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury will play for the Gold Coast Suns next year. Joe Armao Essendon

Key players: Zach Merrett, Jordan Ridley Again, the focus at Bomberland is Merrett, who, for the second-straight season, is seeking a trade to Hawthorn. As reported by this masthead, the Hawks have offered picks 15 and 25 in this year’s draft, along with a future selection – either a second- or third-round draft pick – but the Bombers have rebuffed this. It’s unclear what will satisfy Essendon when it comes to relinquishing their seven-time best-and-fairest, and former skipper. Merrett is contracted for 2027. The Bombers are chasing Melbourne premiership veteran Jack Viney, who could replace Merrett in the midfield. Defender Ridley is on Geelong and North Melbourne’s radar. Out-of-favour Cat Jack Bowes has requested a trade to the Bombers. - Jon Pierik Fremantle Draft picks: 17, 38, 58, 76, 94

Key players: Sean Darcy, Nathan O’Driscoll

Darcy’s future remains a point of debate despite the Dockers insisting the ruckman will remain at the club. He fell out of favour this season with Luke Jackson dominant, while Mason Cox was the preferred second ruck in their finals campaign. Darcy, 28, is contracted until the end of 2030. Wingman O’Driscoll has told the club he is exploring his options, having rejected a three-year contract offer amid interest from the Western Bulldogs. The Dockers say they have not expressed interest in luring ex-Magpie Bobby Hill or Sydney’s Chad Warner home, while their discussions with ex-Tiger Nathan Broad are purely about a coaching role. - Jon Pierik Geelong Draft picks: 14, 34, 55, 73, 91

Key players: Gryan Miers, Jack Bowes The Cats were disappointed to miss out on Zak Butters, but can now use that money to load up on other talent. Giants great Toby Greene officially joined on Friday as a free agent, while they are again haggling with the Saints over a trade for ruckman Rowan Marshall. The Cats have offered pick 32 as the crux of the deal, but St Kilda want Geelong’s top pick. The Cats are also chasing Essendon defender Jordan Ridley, and are open to discussing Nick Blakey, should the Swan be determined to leave the club after the alleged Pullman Hotel incident. Miers has completed a medical at West Coast, but remains keen to stay at Geelong, but Bowes has requested a trade to Essendon. - Jon Pierik Gold Coast

Draft picks: 65, 79, 83

Key players: Charlie Ballard, Ben King (restricted free agent), Jamarra Ugle-Hagan, Matt Rowell King will head to Hawthorn on a seven-year, $9 million deal, but the free agency compensation – pick No.7 – may not satisfy the Suns, who could match the Hawks’ offer and force a trade for the star goal-kicker. Hawk Aidan Schubert could end up being involved. Gold Coast have yet to indicate whether they will offer Ugle-Hagan another one-year deal, while Rowell is an intriguing case. The 2025 Brownlow medallist has a year to run on his contract, and is weighing up a return home to Victoria. If a sweetheart deal was put before the Suns now, would they move early? Gold Coast may need to engineer a late trade to secure unrestricted free agent Scott Pendlebury, so any compensation from the AFL for King is not diluted. Ballard is likely to stay at the club despite rival clubs’ interest. - Jon Pierik GWS Draft picks: 7, 26, 29, 48, 84

Key players: Harry Himmelberg, Jesse Hogan, Jake Stringer, Lachie Whitfield The Giants already decided not to offer contracts to Hogan and Kieren Briggs, and were comfortable with Stringer’s decision to move back to Victoria, but were hoping to retain Toby Greene, who is off to Geelong. Whitfield is poised to become a Blue after completing a medical after GWS were open to shedding his salary as they prioritise their younger group. A fourth-round pick will seal Hogan’s passage to Collingwood early in the trade period, while Briggs joined Richmond on a four-year deal. GWS may look to add more ruck depth and had explored interest in Bulldogs big man Tim English. - Marc McGowan

Hawthorn Draft picks: 15, 25, 27, 35, 69, 92

Key players: Sam Butler, Finn Maginness, Will McCabe, Noah Mraz, Max Ramsden, Aidan Schubert, Jack Scrimshaw They already had some wins when in-demand duo Bailey Macdonald and Calsher Dear re-signed. Ben King and Zach Merrett will be Hawks by the end of the player movement period, but how those deals look remains to be seen. North’s Josh Goater has also requested a trade to Hawthorn. Gold Coast are publicly threatening to match any Hawks free agency offer for King, which would trigger a trade, but that is to be determined – and could impact what Hawthorn can offer Essendon for Merrett. The Bombers are trying to convince the Hawks to include developing defender Mraz in any Merrett deal, but Hawthorn are adamant that won’t happen. Fringe players Butler (West Coast) and Maginness (Western Bulldogs) have opposition interest. - Marc McGowan Melbourne Draft picks: 6, 10, 47, 87

Key players: Trent Rivers, Jack Viney

Advertisement

The Demons missed out on Hawk Calsher Dear, who decided to stay in brown and gold. However, once-prized Roo Zane Duursma wants to join Steven King’s squad and that deal will require some haggling to determine his current value after being the No.4 pick in 2023. Lion Will McLachlan is another possible addition. Viney played just once this past season due mostly to injury, but Melbourne are going in a different midfield direction and encouraged him to explore his options. West Coast and Essendon are duelling for Viney’s signature, and it is unlikely he will net a strong return as effectively a salary dump. Rivers was once considered a big part of Melbourne’s future, but there have been constant murmurings that he might pursue a fresh start this off-season, which is yet to eventuate. - Marc McGowan Jack Viney in action recently. AFL Photos North Melbourne Draft picks: 5, 45, 64, 72, 82

Key players: Zane Duursma, Josh Goater, Tom Powell The Kangaroos’ No.1 off-season target is contracted Adelaide key defender Nick Murray, who they have presented with a five-year contract. That deal rests on the Crows’ willingness to let him go, and what North would offer to tempt them to relinquish defensive depth. Powell is a South Australian, so is often raised a potential part of any Murray trade. Duursma wants to join Melbourne, while Goater is keen to be a Hawk, so the Roos can expect to be busy in this year’s trade period. Contracted Bomber Jordan Ridley is a target, but his preference is believed to be Geelong. They were also keen on Cat Jack Bowes, but he nominated Essendon instead. Could they pivot to players such as Hawthorn’s Jack Scrimshaw and/or Max Ramsden? - Marc McGowan

Advertisement

Port Adelaide Draft picks: 4, 22, 30, 44, 46, 63, 81

Key players: Tom Anastasopoulos, Zak Butters, Ollie Lord, Todd Marshall Butters is the big one here, and specifically, what the Power will garner from his impending move to the Western Bulldogs. They will score pick five if they choose not to match the Dogs’ enormous nine-year deal, worth up to $18 million. That scenario remains a likely outcome, even after the AFL blocked their proposed side trade that involved Marshall also heading to the Kennel, Port paying a large chunk of his salary, and scoring two first-round picks in return. However, league rules prohibit a club losing a free agent from paying the salary of another player going to the same club, for integrity reasons. It is still probable that Marshall is in different colours next year, with both parties open to a move. Crow Luke Pedlar wants to join the Power. - Marc McGowan Richmond Draft picks: 2, 20, 42, 61

Key players: Jayden Short

Advertisement

The Tigers have already bolstered their ruck division with the free agency addition of ex-Giant Kieren Briggs, after they initially pursued his teammate Nick Madden. Briggs inked a four-year deal that positions himself as Richmond’s long-term successor for captain Toby Nankervis. Short is exploring his trade options, including meeting with Collingwood, but this masthead previously confirmed that fellow veteran Nick Vlastuin is not interested in continuing his career elsewhere. They did attempt to recruit Zak Butters, but were never considered as a genuine frontrunner. The Tigers will bring in another top talent in the draft and may be involved in some peripheral trades across the next 10 days. - Marc McGowan St Kilda Draft picks: 8, 49, 67, 85

Key players: Rowan Marshall, Mattaes Phillipou, Alix Tauru St Kilda’s Alix Tauru is talented but raw. Getty Images Fringe Lion Sam Marshall has requested a trade to the Saints, who continue to add secondary players from other clubs as they try to return to the finals. Marshall wanted to join Geelong last year and is again pursuing that move, which should eventuate this time. The Cats have so far knocked back St Kilda’s interest in Lawson Humphries and Sam De Koning, while they are also reluctant to part with their first-round selection. The Tauru saga is a fascinating one, and could still have another twist, but the likeliest outcome is he remains a Saint. Another of St Kilda’s top-10 picks, Phillipou, who is reportedly on a $1 million-a-year salary, was raised in trade dispatches, but club football boss Lenny Hayes denied he was up for grabs. Hayes also revealed it was unlikely they would broker a trade for Bulldog Rory Lobb. - Marc McGowan

That netted Sydney a second-round pick as compensation. The Blakey situation will remain a talking point until it gets shut down. Blakey, who is contracted for five more seasons on a lot of money, is believed to be open to a move to Geelong, but this is a complex situation and any potential deal would require the Cats giving up something significant. - Marc McGowan West Coast

Key players: N/A The Eagles are actively pursuing talent to hasten their rebuild, with Jack Viney, Gryan Miers and Sam Butler among the opposition players on their wish list. They are in a two-way battle with Essendon for Viney, while they have undertaken medical testing on Miers, but he ideally wants to stay at Geelong. Hawthorn’s Butler has never played more than nine games in a season, so could be keen on a fresh start, but is contracted for one more season. Melbourne’s Trent Rivers, who hails from Western Australia and is rumoured to be considering his options, could emerge as a target if he requests a trade from the Demons. - Marc McGowan Western Bulldogs Draft picks: 12, 31, 53, 89

Key players: Tim English, Rory Lobb The Bulldogs already signed ex-Crows defender Jordon Butts in free agency, and superstar midfielder Zak Butters is also headed their way, whether in restricted free agency or a trade with Port Adelaide in a major coup. Out-of-favour Hawk Finn Maginness, who is contracted for 2027, is on the Bulldogs’ radar, while Docker Nathan O’Driscoll could be a name to follow. Michelle Raguz sells freshly made biscuits and cakes on her Instagram account. Source: Supplied / @thewogbox

The NSW Food Authority tells SBS News that "anecdotal feedback from local councils indicates home-based food businesses have grown in number", although it does not specifically collect data on these businesses.

Driven by a mix of nostalgia, convenience and a desire for supportive communities, these micro businesses have also become a way for people to stay connected to their culture, share food traditions and recreate a sense of home.

Not everyone can bake mum's biscuits

Among the Balkan community in Australia, including those of Macedonian and Serbian heritage, it's traditional to enjoy treats like madarice (a chocolate layer cake) and oblatne (wafers) with coffee at social gatherings.

But Raguz says many older members of the Croatian community can no longer make the traditional biscuits and cakes she sells.

"Even my mother-in-law, she's got arthritis in her hands [so] they can't stand there and bake anymore," she says.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, she was spurred to start her business by a desire to help her community, which didn't have the option of having traditional foods delivered.

[During lockdowns] if you wanted to reach out to somebody, the only option people had were … donuts or flowers.

This was not appealing to Croatians, Raguz says, who love having small portions of a variety of homemade cakes and biscuits.

"We're biscuity people. You have a slice of this, or a piece of that."

Raguz spent nearly a year perfecting her almond moons to taste just like the ones her aunt made. Source: Supplied

About 90 per cent of her customers are of Balkan heritage, but she also has other customers who have found her sweet treats after friends or neighbours shared her biscuits with them, for example.

"I actually get a lot of Asians — once they try it, they love it."

Michelle Raguz (centre) says she loves cooking for her family and enjoys keeping Croatian food traditions alive. Source: Supplied

Raguz says she loves recreating the warm memories she had growing up and is lucky to have inherited a love of cooking from her mum.

"All of our friends still talk about my mother's hospitality," she says, adding that she always wanted to carry that on with her own children.

I don't want the way we grew up to be lost.

'Cooked by people that care'

Home cooking can create a sense of care that sets it apart from restaurant meals, says Carol Perdigao, a former chef who moved to Melbourne from Brazil six years ago.

She regularly orders food such as feijão tropeiro (bean stew) and empadão de palmito (palm heart pie) from a home cook via WhatsApp.

"It's something I miss from home," she says of the dishes, which she adds can be difficult to find in Brazilian restaurants in Australia that often focus on meat.

She says that when she began ordering the food she was mainly motivated by the desire to support the Brazilian community in Australia but says it is also "one of the best foods flavour-wise because it's cooked by people that care".

"A lot of people work in hospitality because they end up there and it's a very busy-paced life," Perdigao notes of restaurant cuisine.

"[You don't] necessarily get that sort of care with the food."

The meals have also helped Carol to continue the Brazilian tradition of having a large warm meal for lunch.

"It's an important part of the day for me," she says. "It's a habit that I really wasn't able to get rid of."

I basically don’t feel satisfied if I don’t eat a home-cooked lunch.

Cultural sociologist Sian Supski, a research fellow at Monash University, says food can be used to make people feel at home. She says women migrating to Australia in the 1950s used it as a way to become part of the Australian suburbs.

"They would give food to their neighbours and then their neighbours would ask for the recipes," she says.

Migrants must also find local substitutes for some ingredients and Supski says this creates a lot of "cultural traffic" between the place they now live and where they came from.

"So I think that food helps the placemaking [that helps people feel connected to spaces]."

'I feel like people appreciate me'

Sarah (not her real name) says the thing she values the most about selling her homemade dumplings is that it gives her a chance to meet her neighbours, and a topic to talk about.

"My job [in Australia is] pretty boring and not so many people talk [with me]," she tells SBS News.

"[But] I love chatting."

Sarah sees her dumpling business as just a hobby, which is why she doesn’t want her name to be published. She sells one or two bags of dumplings in Sydney each week, mostly through posts on a local community Facebook page.

"Back in China you have a good income; here you [are] basically nothing," she says.

Doing this just give me confidence. I feel like people appreciate me. I feel good for myself.

Sarah's jiaozi (northern Chinese-style dumplings) are a blend of how her grandma cooks and the preferences of her non-Chinese husband and two children.

The pork and prawn filling is minced by hand chopping, just like Sarah's grandma's, but she wraps them using store-bought dumpling pastry, which is thinner than handmade dough, and steams them rather than boiling them.

This also suits Sarah's customers as the majority of them are not Asian. Regular buyers include a woman who orders dumplings every Valentine's Day, and a man who buys them monthly to serve to his mates during a regular catch-up.

Sarah's jiaozi has helped her to get to know her neighbours. Source: Supplied

Once her children finish their education, Sarah says she may start a small dumpling bar because she loves having a drink and chatting with friends while eating dumplings.

"You know Chinese, we love sharing food," Sarah says.

"The way we show love [to] neighbours or that, we just keep feeding them. That's the Chinese."

Mother-of-three Asma Khalaf would also like to build up her business selling Middle Eastern treats in Sydney.

Khalaf arrived in Australia from Gaza two years ago and the 39-year-old says she wanted to find a way to talk about her background.

How can I show other people, who [are] in different culture, about my culture?

"Then I start thinking about food, because food is the main language to talk about your country."

A former teacher, Khalaf says she used to enjoy making pastries in her spare time before the war.

She's now selling these using Palestinian recipes inspired by her mother through an Instagram account. Eid is the busiest time for her and last year she made 13kg of fragrant treats like maamoul (date cookies), kaak (ring-shaped pastry) and baklava (layered filo pastry dessert).

Asma Khalaf sells Middle Eastern pastries such as maamoul and kaak on her Instagram page. Source: Supplied / @yafasweet__

While most of her goods are sold to those of Middle Eastern background, about 30 per cent are bought by people from other cultures.

Demand can be quite unpredictable but Khalaf hopes to eventually open her own shop, to help support her family in Australia and Gaza.

Supski says food can hold an important role for migrants from countries that have experienced societal upheaval and seen their cultural and literary heritage destroyed.

"They have lost their loved ones, or their connection because records have been lost, as well as people.

"The re-creation of food and the feeding of community is this very direct connection straight back to family or to the place that people grew up."

Concerns over food safety and commercialisation

But the Food Safety Information Council has warned Australians not to buy or sell food through social media sites that is prepared in unregulated home kitchens.

Chief executive officer Lydia Buchtmann says food prepared in a home kitchen or backyard barbecue is unlikely to meet the food safety regulations that apply to businesses selling food.

A NSW Food Authority spokesperson tells SBS News home-based food businesses must meet the same requirements as all food businesses in NSW.

"Home-based businesses must notify the appropriate authority, their local council or the NSW Food Authority, with their business details so their food safety compliance requirements can be assessed," the spokesperson says.

READ MORE The costly contradiction hiding in Australian kitchens

Sukhmani Khorana of the University of NSW, whose research looks at how migrants use food cultures to foster belonging, says food safety verification is important, although she questions whether it's always accessible to the people starting these businesses.

"Sometimes it also doesn't matter a great deal to customers from the same community if they know the family," she tells SBS News.

She says she's also noticed an increase in supper clubs, where people host guests in their homes, which can allow for specific foods from certain regions to be experienced in place of cuisines often served in restaurants catering to broader tastes.

But Khorana notes there is always a potential downside to commercialising any cultural product.

Australia has a long history of multicultural foods starting off as operated and owned by independent families or from ethnic backgrounds, and then becoming cool … [and] too homogenised and commercialised.

She is concerned social media algorithms may also limit access to foods and businesses to those who are already searching for them.

"Opportunities we had before [may have] extended that knowledge and awareness to other communities as well."

Selling food and posting recipes on social media may help provide access to food that is not commonly available — especially to younger generations — but Khorana points out that platforms like Instagram rely heavily on visual aesthetics.

"Not all ethnic food is going to be visually appealing."

Supski acknowledges concerns around the reliance on social media but says it appears to have played a positive role for some people amid concerns about what some say is a loneliness epidemic.

These online communities … bring a lot of connection and support to the people who are selling the food.

title: Flydubai co-pilot used axe in attempted 'terrorist attack', senior UAE official says
text:
IN BRIEF The United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said a recent flydubai incident was an attempted "terrorist attack".

The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with a crash axe, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi also said.

This article contains references to suicide.

The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Israel, attempted to carry out a "terrorist attack" during the flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, according to the state news agency WAM.

The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.

A second source briefed on the investigation confirmed the co-pilot’s name. UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity.

While Emirati authorities have not publicly identified the co-pilot, Israeli officials have previously said he is an Omani national. Oman has not commented on the incident.

"Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack," WAM quoted UAE attorney-general Hamad Saif Al Shamsi as saying.

The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft, the prosecutor general said.

A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies such as crashes.

Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added.

The UAE is leading the investigation. The airline is owned by Dubai's government.

The UAE prosecutor general's comments were the first by Emirati authorities to describe the incident as an attempted terrorist attack.

Disaster was averted on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had attacked the captain in what Israeli officials said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying more than 170 passengers and crew.

A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.

The captain and co-pilot left Saudi Arabia for Abu Dhabi on Thursday morning after receiving medical clearance, the Saudi Interior Ministry said.

Flydubai said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and that it was not in a position to comment further, a spokesperson said.

A source briefed on the investigation told Reuters on Friday that Israeli officials were expected to question the co-pilot in the UAE. The source declined to say which Israeli agency or authority would take part.

An Israeli government official told Reuters that Israeli investigators would take part alongside Emirati authorities in the UAE-led investigation, seeking to determine what happened and examine the suspect's motives and background.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning that anyone involved would pay a "heavy price".

Netanyahu said on Thursday that the co-pilot had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination, without providing details, and appeared suicidal, though he said a motive had not yet been established.

The aircraft dropped about 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia on its journey from the UAE to Israel, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24.

The route is popular among Israeli travellers and most of the passengers on board were Israeli nationals.

title: The common viral infections that are responsible for one in eight cancers
text:
in brief A new global analysis has revealed that 12 per cent of cancer is caused by pathogenic infection.

Just four viruses and one bacteria are responsible, opening new pathways for cancer prevention.

Roughly one in every eight cancer cases diagnosed worldwide is triggered by common viral and bacterial infections, rather than inherited genetics or lifestyle factors.

A major global analysis by the World Health Organization body, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, has found that an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 were directly caused by 12 carcinogenic pathogens.

While developing cancer is often viewed as unpredictable, the findings highlight the fact that millions of cases worldwide come from transmissible infections — which are largely preventable.

In an analysis for The Conversation, Dr John La Marca and Dr Sarah Diepstraten, senior research officers at Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute, noted that the vast majority of these cancer diagnoses are driven by just a handful of pathogens.

"Four viruses and one bacteria were responsible for 12% of the world's cancer cases in 2024," they wrote.

Kate Broun, deputy chair of Cancer Council’s Cancer Screening and Immunisation Committee, told SBS News that vaccinations and screenings can reduce the risk of cancers.

How does an infection cause cancer?

Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow out of control instead of dying, and is one of the leading causes of death worldwide.

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare estimates that around 170,000 new cases of cancer are diagnosed each year in Australia. Roughly 40 per cent of the population will receive a cancer diagnosis by the age of 85.

The disease is caused when normal cell functions are disrupted, something that a virus or a bacterium can trigger.

Certain viruses, like human papillomavirus (HPV), insert their own genetic material directly into human DNA, hijacking cells and deactivating tumour-suppressing proteins. This allows the cells to divide uncontrollably.

"HPV can cause several cancers and other diseases in people of all genders," Broun said. "It is responsible for cases of cervical cancer, anal cancer, vaginal cancer, vulvar cancer, and penile cancer."

Other pathogens, like Helicobacter pylori in the stomach or hepatitis B and C in the liver, operate through persistent, chronic inflammation.

Decades of continuous tissue damage, cell death, and forced regeneration significantly increase the probability of copying errors, which eventually turn healthy cells malignant.

Others still, like HIV, weaken the immune system's natural surveillance mechanisms, which gives other, dormant viruses in the body the chance to activate and trigger tumours.

Which viruses cause cancer?

The report, published in Lancet Oncology, found that four primary pathogens were responsible for the vast majority of infection-driven cancers in 2024.

They were:

H. pylori: A common stomach bacterium responsible for 760,000 cases annually, mainly non-cardia gastric cancers.

HPV: Responsible for 750,000 cases, with cervical cancer making up 600,000 of those diagnoses.

Hepatitis B and C: Driven by chronic liver infections, these caused 360,000 and 160,000 cases of liver cancer, respectively.

Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV): The virus responsible for glandular fever also drove 260,000 cases, with more research needed into its role in throat and stomach cancers, as well as various lymphomas.

Despite being the primary cause behind a substantial number of cancer cases, public awareness of the role pathogens play in the disease is limited.

La Marca and Diepstraten attribute this to the fact that many people carry these pathogens without knowing it.

"These infections can cause more than 20 different types of cancer, including stomach, liver, blood and cervical cancers," they wrote, noting that there is a long delay between infection and cancer onset, which blurs the link.

Preventing future cancer diagnoses

Despite the considerable global figures, researchers emphasise that infection-driven cancers represent the most preventable type on the planet.

Several successful public health interventions for many of these primary pathogens already exist.

HPV and hepatitis B immunisations offer anti-cancer protective properties, while hepatitis C antivirals and antibiotic treatment for H. pylori can eliminate chronic risks before issues develop.

"The HPV vaccine is safe and effective at protecting against HPV-related cancers and diseases," Broun said. "It is recommended and free for Australians aged 12 to 25 years of age."

"Even if you’re vaccinated against HPV, we encourage you to screen."

She added that people uncertain if they have been vaccinated against hepatitis B can speak with their GP about a blood test.

While there is no preventative vaccine against EBV, clinical trials are underway.

"Because these infections are largely preventable or treatable," La Marca and Diepstraten wrote, "scaling up global access to existing vaccines, screening, and antimicrobial therapies offers one of our most direct routes to cutting global cancer rates".
