title: 'Adventurous' escaped capybara stays one step ahead after six months on the lam
text:
IN BRIEF Samba escaped with her sister Tango in March while being held in a temporary enclosure.

Zoo staff have been searching for the capybara for six months, responding to over 150 reported sightings.

Samba the capybara has been on the run for six months after escaping a temporary enclosure at Marwell Zoo in the UK.

Samba arrived at Marwell Zoo in Hampshire County on March 16 with her sister, Tango.

The pair were transferred from Jimmy's Farm and Wildlife Park in Suffolk.

Samba and Tango underwent "routine health checks" while their enclosure was being prepared, Marwell Zoo said in a statement.

The following day, while locked in a temporary holding area, the pair attempted a jailbreak.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Samba and Tango had other ideas ... and managed to escape from their new home," the zoo said.

Staff "quickly retrieved" Tango on zoo grounds. But nine-month-old Samba was "more adventurous" and has now been missing for six months.

The first sighting of Samba came a day after her escape in Owslebury, three kilometres from the zoo.

On 22 March, a dog walker spotted Samba lying in the sun on the banks of the River Itchen in the Colden Common area. Startled by the dog walker, Samba scurried down the banks and jumped into the river, making her escape by water.

She was spotted by the river the very next day.

Search efforts increased around the river, but the capybara's excellent camouflage secured her freedom.

Camera traps were placed in various locations where Samba had been spotted, including Twyford, North Twyford, Highbridge and Bambridge Gardens.

Rescue teams also conducted daily ground searches and thermal drone imaging searches — teams responded to 150 reported sightings.

Zoo insists new male not replacing Samba

On 7 July, Marwell Zoo introduced a new capybara.

Seven-year-old male Ripple was transferred from Blackpool Zoo and gradually introduced to the enclosure with Tango.

"His move is first and foremost about ensuring Tango's continued welfare by providing her with appropriate companionship," Marwell Zoo said.

The introduction of the new capybara raised concerns for Samba's future, but the zoo ensured she was not being replaced.

Ripple, a seven-year-old male capybara, has been introduced to Marwell Zoo as a companion animal for Tango, who was experiencing isolation stress. Source: Getty / Mark Metcalfe

"Welcoming Ripple does not mean we have stopped searching for her," they said.

"Our efforts to find Samba continue, and her welfare remains a priority for the team."

The last known sighting of Samba was on 11 August, near Bambridge Gardens.

Marwell Zoo said its team was "acting on a very promising lead" from photographic evidence of the now year-old capybara.

What are capybaras?

Native to South America, capybaras are the world's largest living rodent. They belong to the Caviidae family and are close relatives of the guinea pig and rock cavy.

They can live anywhere between four and eight years in the wild, and 12 in captivity.

Capybaras are semiaquatic herbivores, meaning they can live across savannas and dense forests and near and in freshwater.

They spend most of their time grazing or swimming and are highly social animals, preferring to live in large, close-knit groups of 10 to 40.

The average capybara weighs between 35 and 70 kilograms and stands about 60 centimetres tall.

Usually a slow and calm rodent, capybaras can have bursts of energy. They can reach speeds of 35km/hour when startled or threatened.

This speed helps them escape predators or, apparently, zookeepers eager to return them to captivity.

title: How daylight saving leaves one Australian border town operating on two different clocks
text:
In brief Daylight saving returns this weekend, renewing calls for southeast Queensland to adopt the time change.

Border businesses near Tweed Heads and Coolangatta are preparing for booking mix-ups and confusion.

Same headache, new year.

In the wee hours of Sunday morning, daylight saving kicks in for the long Australian summer, when clocks skip forward by an hour from 2am to 3am.

But while the citizens of NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia and the ACT will enjoy an extra hour of sunshine after clocking off, Queensland remains the eastern seaboard outlier.

Daylight saving is an annual talking point on the Gold Coast, with Mayor Tom Tate on Wednesday reiterating calls for daylight saving to be introduced in Queensland's southeast corner.

Tate suggested drawing a new time zone boundary north of Noosa — cheekily acknowledging the lack of support elsewhere from cows and the wider dairy industry.

But for businesses in the NSW border town of Tweed Heads, as well as Coolangatta on the Queensland side, the issue is no joke.

Ellen Clark, a cosmetic nurse, recently opened a business in Tweed Heads and is bracing herself for late arrivals from her clientele, most of whom are in Queensland.

"It's going to be interesting trying to navigate that," she told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).

Previously, Ms Clark commuted to Brisbane for work from Tweed Heads, where her partner is based, but decided to set up shop locally after the birth of her first child.

"I used to have to stay on Queensland time while my partner would operate on NSW time," she said.

"It kind of came to my attention yesterday, and I was like, 'Oh my God, we're back here again'."

Sean McMillan is also new to Tweed Heads, having just set up a barber shop on Bay Street.

"All my systems go off bookings, so I'm trying to do some research, and I'm changing my hours a little bit to catch people on both sides of the border," he told the AAP.

"I'm sure there'll be people coming in an hour early or an hour late for bookings ... It's just one of those puzzles to work out."

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli was not keen to buy into Tate's suggestion when asked about the issue by reporters in Mackay on Thursday.

"I've lived at both ends of the state, and I'm here for uniting Queensland, not dividing it," he said.

Queensland trialled daylight saving between 1989 and 1992 before being comprehensively rejected in a state referendum.

title: How one Australian state's corruption inquiry shook a major political party
text:
In brief NSW ICAC’s Operation Rosny examined alleged links between Liberal Party figures and developer Jean Nassif over donations and influence.

The high-profile inquiry exposed damaging allegations ahead of the state election and renewed scrutiny of party fundraising.

Phone calls packed with colourful language, meetings at Nobu, Fijian hideouts, all-day drinks at London pubs, promises of millions of dollars.

It was enough to fill out 38 sitting days as the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) sliced and diced a Liberal Party corruption scandal.

At the heart of the probe, the ICAC examined alleged collusion between fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and party powerbrokers including two brothers of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet.

Jean-Claude Perrottet, Charles Perrottet and his wife Anita Perrottet endured days of grilling in the witness box.

In an inquiry dubbed Operation Rosny, the watchdog investigated alleged kickbacks involving Nassif and his company, Toplace, between 2020 and 2023.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Political donations from developers have been banned in NSW since 2009, yet the ICAC's widening net led to mentions of other powerful Liberals, including federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.

Former ICAC assistant commissioner and retired Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy rates Rosny one of the most impactful investigations in the body's almost 40-year history.

"You can already rank it as a very consequential inquiry," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) news agency.

"That is because it's taking quite a broad swipe into the machinations of party politics, the relationships between developers and politicians and where those intersections can go seriously wrong."

The inquiry began with a bang in July when counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer launched her opening statement with the adage, "Money in politics, as in other spheres of life, has the potential to corrupt."

It ushered in weeks of forensic accounting and questions over embarrassing text exchanges about surveillance of mayors, sham contracts and fake arrangements spanning Beirut, London and Cessnock.

Twenty witnesses were called, including the bombastic Nassif, who dialled in virtually from his bedroom in Beirut, wrapping up on Tuesday.

Their memories — from a demure Jean-Claude Perrottet and emotional senior Liberal MP Damien Tudehope to brash lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood and a befuddled Anita Perrottet — were put to the test on the stand.

In their responses, revelations were unearthed, and admissions recorded that have damaged the Liberal Party as it heads to a state election in March.

"In terms of the Academy Awards, some would be given out for splendid attempts to shy away from the truth without very much success," Whealy says.

"Overall, the spectacle we saw was rather amusing, but then it wasn't amusing at all; it was really quite serious."

He says a number of witnesses have tarnished their reputations by not being open and honest with the commission.

Central to the probe was how the Reformers, a conservative Christian sub-faction within the Liberal Party, allegedly circumvented donation caps by setting up schemes to hide the money trail.

Taylor, who is not under investigation by the corruption watchdog, has denied making pledges to the ultra-conservative faction.

"I want to shake down Angus for 10K," the now sacked head of Catholic Schools NSW, Dallas McInerney, wrote in a message aired at the inquiry on Tuesday.

The opposition leader said "no payment was made" when questioned about a $15,000 "injection" and monthly $3000 donations to the Reformers.

Former NSW premier Nick Greiner doesn't want to wade into how Operation Rosny will affect the party whose federal executive he served until March this year.

But he credits the creation of ICAC in 1989, during his tenure as premier, as one of his most important contributions to keeping politics accountable.

"ICAC is now close to 40 years old, so in a broad sense it's been successful — and the fact that it's been copied everywhere is a fair indication of that," he says.

Its public airing of dirty laundry, which played a role in Greiner's own political demise, later brought down popular Liberal premier Gladys Berejiklian and Labor heavyweight Eddie Obeid.

Yet it has not been immune from criticism.

Greiner says the commission's sometimes spectacular binge-watching sessions were not all necessary.

"There's room for more common sense and discretion," he insists.

But he reserves sterner ire for how long it often takes the ICAC to establish a probe and make corruption findings, and then whether it recommends prosecutions.

The watchdog aims to have a report tabled in parliament within 180 days of receiving final submissions but in practice it takes much longer.

"Clearly the time frames are absolutely absurd," Greiner says.

"It cannot take years and years when you've got all the powers that ICAC has ... My general impression is it's way too slow."

Rosny was sparked when state Liberal MP Ray Williams used parliamentary privilege in 2022 to claim powerbrokers in his party were engaged in branch-stacking and improper local council dealings.

Whealy says the watchdog's invaluable oversight role should reassure the public that no matter how corrupt political parties might appear, there is always a comeuppance.

"There are some rotten apples around and (the ICAC) reinforces that notion but it doesn't destroy trust altogether in the political system," he says.

"It's a comfort to the community ... that there's a vigilant oversight body doing its job properly."

title: The age measure where Australian women outperform men three to one
text:
The Bureau of Statistics revealed this week that there were 188,421 registered deaths in Australia in 2025, which was 0.6 per cent higher than the previous year.

An ageing population contributed, with the median age of death for males at 79.7 years and 84.6 for females.

But what surprised me the most about the statistics is the extent to which females are outliving males, and in far greater numbers.

Among Australians who lived to 100 or older, women far outnumbered men: 2,392 women died last year, compared with 724 men.

That’s more than three women for every man.

So with an ageing population, it's no surprise to hear the corporate regulator ASIC say earlier this week that one of its key priorities this year is to deal with funeral insurance.

It says it continues to receive reports from the Australian Financial Complaints Authority and consumer groups about this type of insurance, especially where costs exceed benefits.

AI makes games more expensive

The Reserve Bank lifted interest rates this week to a 15-year high because it’s worried about rising inflation.

A key factor is how much businesses are passing on higher costs from the war in the Middle East to consumers.

In its official inflation report this week, the ABS said builders are passing on rising labour and material costs to customers via higher project home prices.

But it’s not the only industry passing on rising costs, and not all are related to the conflict.

The ABS also found games, toys and hobbies were 12.7 per cent more expensive in the year to August because price increases in computer chips are being passed on to consumers.

A global rush to invest in artificial intelligence is placing pressure on chip makers to keep up with demand.

So much so, MooMoo chief market strategist Tapas Strickland told me on the SBS On the Money Podcast that one US company was able to lift prices on chips that it rents out by about 20 per cent.

“What Nebius has been able to do, is put through price increases on four-year old Nvidia chips.”

Petrol stations look to electric

You know there’s a structural shift in the car market when traditional petrol companies move toward green energy.

This week Ampol has offered to pay $225 million to buy ultra-fast electric car charging firm Evie Networks.

The proposed merged group would become the largest public DC fast charging network by number of bays in Australia, with around 1,424 DC public charging spots, leapfrogging Tesla which has 1,230.

The deal, however, still needs ACCC approval.

The company says battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales have exceeded 20 per cent of new cars sold on average over the last five months, while public charging infrastructure has lagged BEV uptake.

This comes as the Electric Vehicle Council said a record 103,716 battery electric vehicles were sold in the first half of 2026, along with 54,241 plug-in hybrid electric vehicles.

It did however say EV transition for electric trucks and vans is happening at a crawl, with sales in that category representing less than 1 per cent of their respective markets.

title: 'People start to lose hope': Why more women are turning to elective egg freezing
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

At Jennifer Lynn Salcedo's 36th birthday party, she made an unexpected announcement — she was going to freeze her eggs.

"I didn't realise how empowering it was until I told people that I was doing it," Jennifer tells SBS News.

"I just never really spoke to anyone about actually doing it until I had my birthday ... and was like 'Hey, next week I'm starting this', and everyone just kept asking questions, everyone wanted to know, everyone was curious."

Salcedo says she had been considering egg freezing for around six years. Assisted reproductive technology (ART) involves retrieving and cryopreserving mature, unfertilised eggs — known as mature oocytes — for potential future use.

As women age and the number and quality of eggs naturally decline, freezing eggs can preserve the potential to use younger eggs later. But experts say it doesn't guarantee a future pregnancy or birth, and success depends on factors including the woman's age when the eggs are frozen and the number of eggs stored.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

For Salcedo, who says she has focused on her career in recent years and is currently single, egg freezing has provided an "insurance policy".

I've got a lot of friends that are having children, getting married and ... it's something that I've always wanted to do. It's just not been where my life has taken me.

For women considering egg freezing, the decision can involve balancing age-related fertility decline with the treatment's cost, physical demands and uncertain chances of ultimately using the frozen eggs — raising questions about how much reassurance the technology can realistically provide.

Why more women are considering fertility preservation

Australia's first baby conceived through in vitro fertilisation (IVF) was born in 1980.

Today, ART is an established part of fertility care in Australia, with about one in 16 babies being born as a result of assisted reproductive technology, according to information published by the government-funded platform YourIVFSuccess.

Tamara Hunter is a Perth-based reproductive endocrinology and fertility specialist and believes more women are choosing to freeze their eggs for elective, or non-medical reasons.

She sees women like Salcedo daily and says she also turns away some young women.

"For whatever reason, they've asked their GP to perform a test of their ovarian reserve," Hunter tells SBS News.

"Then, they'll come in with that level, going 'I need to freeze my eggs'. [To] some of them, I'll say, 'Actually, you're 25, your egg count is within the normal range, there's no hurry. Why don't you come back and see me when you're 30?'"

But a woman's egg count is only part of the fertility picture. Ovarian reserve tests can indicate the number of eggs remaining, but they cannot measure egg quality or reliably predict a woman's chances of conceiving naturally.

A study led by researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles, published last year, analysed elective egg-freezing rates in the United States between 2014 and 2021. It found the number of planned elective egg-freezing cycles increased from 4,153 in 2014 to 16,436 in 2021. Among women who froze their eggs between 2014 and 2016, 5.7 per cent returned to use them within the study's five-to-seven-year follow-up period.

But as elective egg freezing has become more common, researchers are still working to understand how frozen eggs perform over longer storage periods.

Hunter says it's unclear whether the amount of time an egg is frozen affects fertility.

We just don't have the large studies to be able to show that ... if you leave it [eggs] frozen for more than five years, it's going to be significantly degraded.

She says that's because data has historically drawn from the women who freeze their eggs for medical reasons, including women whose fertility was at risk from treatments such as chemotherapy, making it difficult to apply some of those findings directly to women who freeze their eggs electively.

Dr Tamara Hunter says it's unclear whether an egg's fertility is affected by how long it is frozen. Source: Getty / Science Photo Library

Modern egg-freezing techniques have also changed the evidence base. Vitrification — a rapid freezing technique — has improved the survival of eggs and embryos during freezing and thawing, although researchers say long-term outcome data for planned egg freezing are still developing.

But professor Georgina Chambers, director of the National Perinatal Epidemiology and Statistics Unit at the University of New South Wales, says modern freezing techniques have produced strong results for embryos.

"We get very good success rates from frozen embryos. How long can they be stored? We're not sure yet, but we know that with modern freezing techniques that are called vitrification ... the quality of those frozen embryos remains extremely high," she tells SBS News.

Chambers is also a lead author of a report which tracked ART treatment practices, pregnancy and birth outcomes across Australia and New Zealand.

The 2024 Australian and New Zealand Assisted Reproduction Database report recorded more than 113,000 IVF treatment cycles in 2024, resulting in more than 20,900 babies. It also found three in four IVF babies were born using frozen embryos, reflecting a clear shift towards frozen embryo transfers.

Chambers says freezing embryos can allow a woman's body to return to a natural cycle before the embryo is transferred, which can improve treatment outcomes.

"We allow the woman's body to return to a natural cycle, where her endometrium is ready to receive that embryo, and we get higher success rates from that process."

How much does egg freezing cost?

In Australia, elective egg freezing is usually self-funded, although costs vary between clinics and some medically indicated fertility-preservation treatment may attract Medicare rebates.

A single egg freezing cycle can cost several thousand dollars, with the total depending on what is included in the clinic's fee, as well as medication, anaesthetist, hospital and storage costs. YourIVFSuccess estimates elective egg freezing typically costs between $8,000 and $12,000 per cycle upfront, with additional annual storage fees.

The cost of using the eggs later is separate. The eggs must be thawed and fertilised to create embryos that are transferred to the uterus, creating further treatment and out-of-pocket expenses.

Jennifer Lynn Salcedo says she also experienced a hormone "crash" after the egg retrieval due to a temporary increase in her estrogen levels. Credit: Jennifer Lynn Salcedo

In September, Salcedo underwent her second egg freezing cycle via a private fertility specialist. Working in the banking sector, she was entitled to five days of family planning leave but admits the process was physically and emotionally taxing.

In my first cycle, I was just hungry, constantly hungry. I gained 7kg in that time from start to extraction, and I was like, 'Oh my god, my body's completely changed'.

Egg freezing requires women to administer daily hormone injections for about two weeks to stimulate the ovaries. The eggs are then collected during a procedure performed under sedation or anaesthesia.

"I was pretty much so bloated that I looked like I was six months pregnant," Salcedo says.

The 'egg count' test

Luke Grzeskowiak is a practitioner fellow at Flinders University's College of Medicine and Public Health and recently published a study analysing almost 1.4 million health records for Australian women.

The study found that anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) tests in Australian general practice increased more than 13-fold between 2011 and 2021. Women aged 30 to 34 recorded the sharpest increase, with testing rates rising almost 20-fold.

AMH is often marketed as a fertility test or "egg count" because it provides an indication of ovarian reserve — the number of eggs remaining in the ovaries.

"AMH testing can tell you about the quantity of eggs remaining, and the largest predictor of that is really just age-related. So, as we get older, there's a natural decline in egg count," Grzeskowiak tells SBS News.

The issue is it can't tell you anything about the quality, and it's really the quality that is the most important predictor of a potential good pregnancy outcome.

Grzeskowiak believes that rise in testing can be attributed in part to increased consumer marketing and ads about AMH.

"There's some interesting research that's published that's evaluated what's marketed around these tests, and what they find is a high level of misinformation around what AMH tests can and can't tell you and their usefulness or potential lack thereof," he says.

He acknowledges AMH testing can have a clinical role, including for people undergoing ART or cancer treatment and can also form part of the assessment of conditions such as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome — formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome — a hormonal condition that can affect the ovaries and reproductive health.

What happens to frozen eggs that aren't used?

As a clinician, Hunter says the rise in elective egg freezing also poses complex ethical questions around the storage and disposal of unused eggs.

We've got this unique irony where we're growing these banks of eggs, and at some point, there won't be enough room.

"So, we've got this opportunity then to talk to young women about, 'Well, you're not going to use them, would you consider donating them?'" she says.

"In that space, there are a lot of ethical and societal challenges: how do we compensate women who've frozen their eggs and paid storage every year for 10 years?"

Unlike IVF treatment for infertility, Medicare does not subsidise elective egg freezing for non-medical reasons. Source: AP / Thanassis Stavrakis

The rules governing how long eggs, sperm (also called gametes) and embryos can be stored vary between Australian states and territories.

Some jurisdictions regulate storage and removal, including for donated gametes or embryos and in circumstances where a donor dies. Other jurisdictions, including the Northern Territory, do not have specific ART legislation.

"In Western Australia you can store them for 10 years and then beyond that we have to ask, 'Do you want to dispose of them ... do you want to donate them?'" Hunter says.

We're not having those discussions with young women who are egg freezing, and that's a problem.

In June last year, health ministers called for a rapid review into ART regulation and accreditation following concerns about "safety, oversight and transparency" in the sector. The review followed two high-profile cases in which embryos were mistakenly transferred.

In September 2025, the review released 10 recommended areas for reform, including changes to how ART services are accredited and regulated.

The Department of Health says the new national standards aim to better align with state-based legislation and regulation, including requirements for the storage and disposal of reproductive material.

A transition to the new scheme is expected by December 2028, with the current regulatory framework to remain in place until then.

In a statement to SBS News, the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) said it provides "ethical guidance for the use of ART in clinical practice and research" through its guidelines, which also set "out the ethical responsibilities of IVF clinics regarding stored gametes and embryos".

However, the NHMRC said the regulation of ART clinical practice is a matter for state and territory governments.

Meanwhile, for women like Salcedo, egg freezing continues to provide a sense of long-term security.

"I think when I get to 40, I'll probably decide if I want to choose to be a single mum and do that, but I'm leaving that decision until later.

"I think a lot of people start to lose hope, especially if you start to get closer to 40, but there are ways to achieve that."

title: New student visa crackdown comes with extra cost for course-switchers
text:
In Brief Students switching education providers will have to pay a new visa fee, expected to cost about half the original visa fee.

Student visa application fees have also risen from $1,600 to $2,000.

New rules for international students are in force, aimed at stopping so-called 'visa-hopping' by limiting course changes and curtailing how family members can join them in Australia.

Students wanting to change education providers will need to apply for a new visa, starting next year, which will cost over $2,000.

Labor's plan to bring net overseas migration down to a budget target of 225,000 by 2028 will be partly fulfilled by closing onshore pathways from temporary visas to student visas, Assistant Citizenship Minister Julian Hill told a migration conference on Friday.

"People will no longer be able to apply for a student visa while in Australia from working holidaymaker visas, training visas, temporary employer visas and so on," he said.

The plan includes banning student and graduate visa holders from bringing their families unless they are on government scholarships, PhD students or from Pacific and ASEAN countries. The new family rules mean that dependants can only be added after their visa is granted.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Families already in Australia will be grandfathered as an exception as the government is not in the business of breaking up families already here," Hill said.

From July next year, students switching education providers will need to apply for a new visa, expected to cost about half the original visa fee, estimated at around $2,500.

The new visa will retain the original end date and can only be issued if students move into equivalent or higher qualifications.

International students who swap courses will have to complete 12 months instead of the current six while the new visa regime is set up.

"Australia welcomes genuine students seeking a premium Australian education but the government will not back down from seeking to manage the size and the shape of the onshore student market," Hill said.

Student visa rejections hit record levels in August at 35 per cent, up 12 per cent on the same month last year.

Students can extend their visa to complete a course if they fall sick, fail a subject or their course provider goes out of business.

After completing a course, they can apply for a new student visa, but it must be ranked higher in the Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF). Moving from higher education to higher VET courses will not be allowed.

Independent MP Allegra Spender told SBS News that temporary visa holders have grown from 1.8 million to 2.8 million in a decade, which is supported by Department of Home Affairs figures.

"That's not sustainable, economically or socially," Spender said.

"International students bring enormous value. But in some universities their growth has coincided with a declining student experience.

"The government must get the settings right, and universities must build a shared campus life, so it's a genuine exchange. Limits to family visas for international students and restrictions on visa hopping are sensible. The question is why these settings are new," she said.

"Every migration choice is a trade-off, and Australians deserve a say in making them. The crossbench will take those trade-offs directly to our communities ... I suspect we'll find far more common ground than the loudest voices suggest."

As a transition measure, transfers have been prevented within the first 12 months of commencing a principal course between now and 1 July 2027, when the new transfer visa comes into effect.

Hill also said there will be a "sharpening focus of the skilled migration program" via two new ministerial directions that came into effect last week.

"Priority is now being given to healthcare, construction, teaching, resources, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing, helping direct skills to the parts of the economy where they are needed most," he said.

The Opposition is expected to announce its immigration policy next week, while One Nation plans to limit net overseas migration to 130,000 per year after three years of "negative migration".

title: Which super funds earned a retirement tick of approval?
text:
in brief An industry assessment handed eight ticks of approval to 45 assessed super funds.

Those eight were found to offer their members the best support through their retirement.

Only eight of 45 assessed superannuation funds have received an industry tick of approval for the level of support they provide members throughout retirement.

The 2026 Epic Retirement Tick has been awarded to retirement funds that met at least 14 of an expanded 20 support criteria, up from 18 last year.

The analysis is backed by Chant West, one of Australia's most prominent commercial superannuation research and ratings agencies.

The tick measures how well a fund's investments perform, how competitive its fees are, how innovative its product offerings are, and how comprehensive its member services and advice are.

"Australians have spent decades building their super," said Epic Retirement Institute founder Bec Wilson.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"As they reach retirement, they deserve to understand what their fund can actually do to support them through the years ahead."

The push for better fund support comes as many Australians approach retirement facing significant savings shortfalls.

According to the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia, a single homeowner requires $630,000 and a couple $730,000 in super for a "comfortable" retirement.

However, Australian Taxation Office data reveal that the median super balance for those aged 60 to 64 is just over $200,000 — meaning retirees rely heavily on fund advice, tax strategies, and government pension integration to stretch their savings.

Wilson noted that the tick is not a product ranking or a directive to switch membership.

"The Tick is not a rating, ranking or recommendation of a super fund or financial product. There's no first place, second place or 'best fund'," she said.

Instead, it serves as a tool to help Australians "become a more informed super fund member and customer".

Which super funds received the Epic Retirement Tick?

Of 45 assessed regulated, defined-contribution funds, only eight met the benchmark for the 2026/2027 financial year.

Those were:

AMP Super

ART-Super Savings

Aware Super

Brighter Super

Colonial First State - FirstChoice

Hostplus

UniSuper

Vision Super

These funds performed well in several distinct categories, like tailored pension investment options, digital security, and advice access.

AMP, ART, Aware, Hostplus, and Vision Super were highlighted for allowing pension members to request ad-hoc payments and receive funds on the same day or via immediate OSKO transfers.

Funds like ART, AMP, and UniSuper also stood out for offering dedicated lifetime income options like annuities to provide members with guaranteed retirement income.

READ MORE There's another reason to check who inherits your superannuation

However, industry analysts note that the overall pass rate remains remarkably low.

Writing in Investment Magazine, Chant West general manager Ian Fryer highlighted that, to earn the badge, funds could no longer rely solely on offering specialised retirement products but also had to demonstrate meaningful member engagement.

For example, funds offering lifetime income options were assessed on whether their members were actually taking up those products.

What has changed this year?

Now in its second year, the Epic Retirement Tick has been awarded to three new funds in addition to last year's six — TelstraSuper having merged with Aware. AMP, Colonial, and Vision are all new additions to the benchmark.

The assessment framework has also been updated to target industry difficulties and raise consumer standards. The pass threshold was raised from 12 out of 18 to 14 out of 20, with a new requirement that funds have no outstanding regulatory enforcement actions.

The expanded 2026 criteria introduced tougher hurdles around digital service delivery, complaints management, and cybersecurity protections.

Investment performance criteria were refined to focus on a seven-year evaluation window, rather than 10 years, to allow a stronger emphasis on non-investment support features.

"Some have really stepped up to the plate," Wilson said. "Others are still working towards the standard, and there remains a meaningful gap between what some funds currently provide and what the criteria ask of them."

The Epic Retirement Tick is a proprietary badge issued by a private research firm, not a binding compliance benchmark.

It is separate to statutory government assessment through the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority.

The property sold on the first weekend of auctions since the September interest rate rise, and since new laws were introduced around the disclosure of sale prices, comparable sales and reserve prices. Weeks later, he ignited a public feud with President Donald Trump, finding himself outside the president’s small decision-making circle. The world’s weathiest man has been appointed to a US committee on the future of warfare. Bloomberg Now Musk has been announced as one of three members of a new Pentagon commission tasked with mapping the future of American warfare, alongside former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, chief executive of military technology company Anduril.

Advertisement

Project Meridian marks a new step in a political transformation larger than any of those men, shifting important responsibility away from democratic government. Rather than privatising how the state operates, Trump’s Washington is now testing the privatisation of decisions about what the state will need. Beginning in 1980, the Reagan administration redrew the line between the private and public sector. Services once seen as the duty of a responsible government were entrusted to the open market, which could price them as they saw fit. Despite the logging of the pillars of government, judgment remained the core responsibility of the state. Companies could sell to the government, but the companies did not decide what a defence strategy required. Project Meridian moves this line yet again.

Advertisement

The old relationship between defence and industry is falling apart. It used to point from requirements, set by the government, to capabilities, built by private companies. Now, the same firms and technologies (including artificial intelligence) cover much more territory on either side of the dividing line between civilian and defence than they did before. A Fury autonomous fighter jet inside Anduril’s California headquarters. Chris Zappone Musk and Luckey lead companies with a combined $US53 billion ($76 billion) in Pentagon contracts and are now tasked with identifying the capabilities that the US military should develop to fight the battles of the future. Luckey described his company’s business model as using “our own money to decide what products to build, how to build then, then we build those products, then we sell them to the government”. He is now one of three people tasked with defining exactly what the government wants to buy.

Advertisement

The neoliberal dream of the 1970s resulted in private companies taking on public tasks. We are now seeing the privatisation of strategic imagination. But governments and businesses are not meant to do the same thing. Navies should not be designed to run a profit. Nor should prisons or hospitals. Governments exist to weigh the interest of its citizens above all else, including alliances and the risk of war itself. This project is part of a longer strategy played out by the Trump administration. In the opening weeks of his second term, Trump signed executive orders making the sale and export of American weapons a top diplomatic and trade priority, to be hawked by American embassies and consulates abroad. The America First Arms Transfer Strategy published this year by the White House says American arms deals are a core part of American foreign policy, used to expand production at home. The administration even made a handy catalogue of items that it encourages allies to acquire, cheapening the highwire task of diplomacy in the 21st century to selling expensive weapons.

Advertisement

The strategy doesn’t stop at bombs. Earlier this year, Trump signed another executive order, declaring another foreign policy goal of the administration to get other countries to adopt American AI technology. Related Article AI Trump rejects AI laws after tech titans agree to ‘self-police’ AI development An ally buying an American F-35 fighter jet is one thing. An ally building its military decision-making capability around American AI models is more tightly wound. As allies become more dependent on American technology, the question of who gets to define the priorities of that technology becomes extremely important. That was made painfully obvious last month with news about OpenAI, a company with deep ties to the White House, gaining unauthorised access to Australian government systems without any human direction.

Advertisement

The stakes for Australia stretch wide. One step below the famous submarines of the AUKUS deal is Pillar II, which focuses on building technological capabilities. It’s designed to make the Australian, British and American militaries work more closely together. The three countries are already jointly testing autonomous systems. They’re sharing sensitive data, and refining how new cutting-edge technology works, together. Integration of the old generation meant ensuring that ammunition from one country could fire in the guns of another. Today, it’s about making sure their software and sensors can talk to each other. A change in how America decides what future military power should look like becomes a change in the assumptions around which Australian defence capability is built. For the past five years, the controversy around AUKUS has been whether it makes Australia too materially dependent on American shipbuilding. The question is now whether Australia is too dependent on American decisions about the future of warfare itself.

Advertisement

The final decisions on how to act and where still reside in Canberra. But the recommendations made by Musk, Luckey and Gingrich will shape the options available. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump is back announcing a 2028 presidential bid. It’s not a joke Cory Alpert Former White House staffer That is, ultimately, why the spectacle of American politics matters so much here, thousands of kilometres away. The decisions made in small rooms in Washington affect how allies, dependent on American systems, can operate. While Reagan’s revolution asked how much the government was needed, this new strategy asks how much decision-making power still belongs to government itself? AUKUS and other alliances mean these questions will not just stay on one side of the Pacific.

Advertisement

Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne looking at the impact of AI on democracy. He previously served the Biden-Harris administration. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

title: WA households are feeling the pinch and making cuts – and one sector will face the most pain
text:
Advertisement

NationalWAAustralian economy WA households are feeling the pinch and making cuts – and one sector will face the most pain Cameron Myles October 4, 2026 — 4:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A new survey has painted a grim picture for Western Australia’s hospitality sector, with households in a glum mood about the rising cost of living and readying to tighten their belts even before the Reserve Bank hiked up interest rates to a 15-year high on Tuesday. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry WA released its September Consumer Confidence survey on Sunday, with almost two in five households surveyed reporting that their expenses outpaced their income each month. WA households are tightening their budgets, and that means cutting back on cappuccinos. Getty Of the 1000 West Australian households surveyed in mid-August, 20 per cent said they had been unable to pay their bills on time, and about half reported they would cut discretionary spending to offset cost-of-living concerns. CCIWA chief economist Dr Daniel Kiely said the hospitality sector would bear the brunt of those discretionary spending cuts.

Advertisement

“Fifty-eight per cent of those surveyed saying they would cut spending on cafes and restaurants over the next six months, which could have a significant impact on the sector heading into the festive period,” he said. Related Article Property prices Why Perth’s housing slump won’t bring relief for everyday buyers “Many consumers have told us they also planned to reduce spending on socialising, with 55 per cent saying they’d spend less at bars, pubs and clubs.” Six in 10 households surveyed reported that interest rates were weighing heavily on their confidence, Kiely said. Their fears were realised on Tuesday, when the RBA board lifted rates to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent.

Advertisement

The move meant a household with a mortgage of $600,000 would be paying another $91 a month, bringing the cumulative increase from the four rate hikes in 2026 to $364. Shadow Treasurer Sandra Brewer said every family across the state had less money than they did five years ago. Speaking to media on Sunday, Brewer took the opportunity to place at least some of the blame at the feet of the Cook government, saying government expenditure was helping drive up inflation. The national consumer price index rose from 3.5 per cent in July to 4 per cent in August, which economists have predicted will keep pressure on the Reserve Bank to push rates higher yet again. Housing costs were the biggest contributor to national annual inflation. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported the cost of new dwellings rose 5.4 per cent in the 12 months to August.

Advertisement

Meanwhile, high global oil prices and the end of the federal fuel excise cut saw transport costs rise 5.6 per cent, which was the second-biggest contributor to inflation. “The best thing government can do is to try and bring inflation down, and that’s by reducing demand in the economy,” Brewer said. “It’s to reduce government spending at a time that the private sector is investing. “So at the moment, last year we had general government expenditure grow by 11 per cent. “In the coming year, it’s forecast to grow at over 8 per cent.

Advertisement

“And we wonder why we can’t get on top of inflation. It’s because Treasurer Rita Saffioti simply won’t pull back. It’s within her power to do so, but she can’t, and she won’t.” Brewer took aim at the government’s “pet projects” – the controversial Burswood racetrack and funding for the Perth Bears NRL team to start up in 2027 among them – and even linked the current inflationary environment to the One Nation byelection shock in Secret Harbour. “People are angry everywhere,” she said. “I think the recent election result in Secret Harbour showed it doesn’t matter what the government says and tells them what a great economy we have, when people are $128 a week worse off for every full-time worker, they know what that means for them and their family.” with Matt Wade

title: Hilary McPhee: The publishing giant who gave rise to Helen Garner, Tim Winton and many more
text:
Advertisement

CultureBooksLiterature Hilary McPhee: The publishing giant who gave rise to Helen Garner, Tim Winton and many more Lauren Ironmonger October 4, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hilary McPhee – a legend of the Australian literary industry who nurtured the careers of writers including Helen Garner and Tim Winton – died on Thursday, aged 85. McPhee Gribble, the publishing house she founded with Diana Gribble in 1975, shaped a generation of iconic Australian writers – among them Kathy Lette, Dorothy Hewett, Kaz Cooke, Drusilla Modjeska, Jennifer Dabbs and John Misto. Their slate of influential novels includes Winton’s Cloudstreet, Garner’s Monkey Grip and Lette and Gabrielle Carey’s Puberty Blues. Writer and editor Hilary McPhee founded McPhee Gribble Publishers with Diana Gribble in 1975. “I published my first four books with McPhee Gribble. Hilary was a fine editor. I’ll always be grateful for that,” says Garner. Winton was just 24 when he first walked into the McPhee Gribble offices, housed in a converted factory in Melbourne’s Fitzroy. The young novelist had come to the publishers by way of literary agent Caroline Lurie, after his first publishers Allen & Unwin didn’t want him to write a collection of short stories.

Advertisement

“I was excited and daunted,” says Winton of their first meeting. He was already aware of McPhee’s prowess as the publisher of Monkey Grip. Editor's pick Review How two women changed the patriarchal world of Australian publishing With Winton working from Western Australia, much of their decades-long partnership unfolded through letters. The pair were corresponding until not long before her death, reminiscing about their time together. “Her handwriting is very familiar to me, it was always pencil on the page, and she was a sensitive and canny editor. She knew when to push, and she was someone you could trust,” says Winton. He recalls McPhee showing up unexpectedly at a reading of his in 2024 for his novel Juice.

Advertisement

“She didn’t have any airs and graces, you know, there was the great Hilary McPhee waiting for it to be signed. And she wrote to me afterwards saying how proud she was and how pleased she was to be there.” Tim Winton pictured in 1984, the year he first won the Miles Franklin award. Together, McPhee and Gribble were trailblazers in the old boys club of Australian publishing. As McPhee wrote in her 2019 memoir Other People’s Words: “The strong men in publishing liked to call in the late afternoons with bottles of wine and kindly advice: stick to packaging, do horse books or ballet books … put together some recipes … get a good-looking, famous sheila to front them for you …” Nikki Christer, a publisher who inherited Picador from McPhee (and its writers such as Winton, Lily Brett and Kate Grenville), describes her predecessor and mentor as a “curious”, “loyal” and “incredibly generous” editor with a “deep respect for the writer’s voice”. “She was part of a generation that transformed Australian publishing. When she and Di created McPhee Gribble, it was largely dominated by overseas publishers and imported books. And so she helped create a publishing culture that put Australian writers and therefore Australian stories at the centre,” she says.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Literature 'The solitude was terrifying': Hilary McPhee on learning to be alone In 2001, Christer published McPhee’s first memoir, Other People’s Words. “It was a really interesting experience to be on the other side of the great editor who then became the writer. She had her own ideas about it … I did find I was slightly intimidated by her as I think we all were. Not that she made you intimidated, she just was a grand figure of Australian publishing,” Christer recalls. “She had that way of looking at you where she would close her eyes and lift her chin, and you would know that you’d said something stupid. She didn’t suffer fools.” McPhee is survived by three children – Sara, Rupert and John. Her business partner and friend, Diana Gribble, died in 2011.

Advertisement

Born in Melbourne in 1941, McPhee’s first foray into the world of publishing was as an editorial assistant at literary journal Meanjin, while studying history and literature at The University of Melbourne. During these student years, she cultivated wide interests, including launching a small magazine, Theatre, and embarking on archaeological expeditions. In 1964 – her final year at university – McPhee married artist Peter Freeman, with whom she would have two children. The pair travelled around Europe and the Middle East before settling in London for a time where McPhee worked at the British Council compiling exhibition books. McPhee in 2001. Craig Abraham

Advertisement

Returning to Australia in 1969, McPhee worked at Penguin Australia, then McKinsey management consulting firm as their first female writer, before starting her own publishing house with Gribble, whom she had met through the women’s movement. Both young mothers, their Fitzroy offices had a crèche, unusual for the time. “When they got too adventurous – climbing out windows and appearing naked on the first floor, escaping from their childminder – they were sent to childcare very quickly. But for quite a while, we did have children in the office, and it was wonderful having them there. We had a nursery that they slept in and a marvellous woman who’d raised six children looking after them,” McPhee told Kill Your Darlings earlier this year. A licensing arrangement with Penguin, publishing the hit children’s book series Practical Puffins (which went on to sell three million copies worldwide), helped keep them afloat in their early years as they set about platforming young Australian voices. The pair published hundreds of titles under their imprint, including those of young Indigenous authors, and fostering the fledgling careers of editors and publishers like Sophie Cunningham and Sue Hines.

Advertisement

Speaking to this masthead in 2022, 46 years after a then unknown Helen Garner walked into their offices, McPhee said: Editor's pick Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos. Literature ‘A poet in plain prose’: Reflections on Helen Garner’s amazing opus “Helen arrived one day on her bicycle with two copies of the manuscript of Monkey Grip in green foolscap folders. This is what writers did in those days, you gave publishers two copies. Di and I each took a manuscript home, read it overnight and rushed in the next day and said we’ve got to publish it.” In 1979, McPhee, Gribble, Joyce Nicholson, Anne O’Donovan and Sally Milner founded Sisters Publishing, a mail order feminist book club that published poetry and fiction “by women, for women”. But by the 1980s, recession hit the Australian publishing industry and the pair signed a co-publishing deal with Penguin before selling McPhee Gribble entirely to Penguin in 1989.

Advertisement

McPhee stayed on for a few years before moving to Pan Macmillan, where she ran the Picador imprint until 1994 when she was headhunted by then prime minister Paul Keating to become the first female chair of the Australian Arts Council. There, she played an instrumental role during a turbulent time for the council – leading a controversial restructuring under Keating. After John Howard was elected prime minister in 1996, he attempted to shut the council down, a feat which McPhee later said embarrassed her terribly when she received an Order of Australia for her services to literature in 2003. As well as penning two memoirs, McPhee published Wordlines (2010), a selection of contemporary Australian writing, and an annotated edition of filmmaker Tim Burstall’s 1950s diaries, Memoirs of a Young Bastard. In 1998, she received an honorary doctorate of letters from Monash University. She served on the judging panel of prestigious awards including the Miles Franklin Literary Award, the Victorian Premiers Award and the Melbourne Prize, and was director and acting editor for a time of online political journal New Matilda.

Advertisement

In 2006, fleeing a failed marriage, McPhee moved halfway around the world, chasing a writing project in the Middle East and immersing herself in the lives of other, solo-living women in Italy and England. She detailed the terrifying solitude of this time in her memoir Other People’s Homes. The Australian publishing industry may not look quite the same as it did in 1976, when McPhee entered the scene, but it’s no doubt all the better thanks to her sharp eye and fierce belief in the people who make it what it is. Her enormous legacy lives on in the pages of Cloudstreet, The Children’s Bach (McPhee’s favourite of Garner’s works) and countless others. title: This 345-kilometre undersea power cable will power Victoria but may ruin dairy farmers
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaRenewables This 345-kilometre undersea power cable will power Victoria but may ruin dairy farmers Benjamin Preiss October 4, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To the untrained eye, the disruption to Paul Peluso’s property from a major interstate electricity transmission line seems minor, perhaps even lucrative. Peluso’s dairy farm lies in the proposed path of the Marinus Link project, which includes 345 kilometres of power and data cables running from north-west Tasmania to the Latrobe Valley in Victoria. The cables will run beneath the Bass Strait and continue underground in Victoria. Whether they want to or not, many Victorian landholders including Peluso will host them. Paul Peluso on his dairy farm. Joe Armao It is crucial national infrastructure for electricity sharing between states, its backers say. But Peluso fears the four-hectare easement on his 180-hectare farm will ruin his dairy business in Mirboo North.

Advertisement

“What they’re proposing to do will shut me down as a dairy farmer,” he said. Marinus Link will dig a trench for the cables and has a six-year window to access his land. Peluso said this would cut across tracks his cows used to move between paddocks and milking sheds. “These main tracks are the arteries that pump the animals to where they need to be.” The vessel, Leonardo da Vinci, will be used to lay the Marinus Link electricity cable between Tasmania and Victoria. Peluso said Marinus Link had made an initial compensation offer during the construction period, in addition to $8000 per kilometre annually on his property for 25 years.

Advertisement

Peluso declined to disclose the construction payment offer, but he said it paled into insignificance against the losses he expected to incur. He is not alone. Many farmers have raised concerns about Marinus Link’s impact on their operations. Peluso’s niece and former Victorian Farmers Federation president, Emma Germano, said real estate agents had advised there would be little interest from buyers in her uncle’s farm while there was uncertainty about the construction works and easement. Emma Germano and her uncle, Paul Peluso, with dog Bonnie, are worried about Marinus Link’s impact on his farm. Joe Armao Germano, who is helping Peluso negotiate fair compensation, said the plans would hurt the farm’s value.

Advertisement

“Why would you buy this dairy farm when you can buy somewhere else with no easement and no construction?” she said. The easement crosses where Peluso loads cattle, but Germano said Marinus Link had rejected a request to move it to a back fence to minimise disruption. Although the cables will be buried, Germano said water movement on the property would be permanently altered and soil disturbances could hamper grass growth. She said there was a power imbalance, making it difficult for farmers to engage in fair compensation negotiations with a big company. The underground cables will run through Paul Peluso’s property. Joe Armao A Marinus Link spokesman said it had engaged with landholders since 2019, including discussions about the route through their land, and was committed to respectful negotiations. He said the company would resort to compulsory acquisition only when absolutely necessary.

Advertisement

The spokesman said the length of time the company needed on each parcel of land depended on many factors from weather to geotechnical conditions. “The best thing we can do is have really open discussions with each landholder on what this will mean for them,” he said. The spokesman said land access involved more than construction and was required for engineering and technical design surveys, and environmental and cultural heritage considerations. An image of a Hitachi valve hall at a converter station in Europe. Marinus Link will consist of two Hitachi valve halls in Tasmania and Victoria to house the electronics that will convert alternating current to direct current and vice versa. In addition to power and fibre-optic cables, Marinus Link will include a communications station and converter stations on both sides of the Bass Strait.

Advertisement

It has attracted less controversy than above-ground projects VNI West and Western Renewables Link, where communities have railed against soaring towers. Related Article Renewables The 345km undersea cable that will help Australia move on from coal The Victorian government approved the environmental effects statement for Western Renewables Link, but Premier Ben Carroll ordered a cost review, raising questions about its future. The Marinus Link cables will run 255 kilometres undersea in Bass Strait and 90 kilometres underground in Gippsland, crossing the shore at Waratah Bay and then on to Latrobe Valley. The federal, Victorian and Tasmanian governments are partners in the venture. The first stage of Marinus Link will have 750-megawatt capacity – enough to power about 750,000 homes.

Advertisement

Tasmania can generate power with its hydroelectric dams, allowing power to flow to Victoria when needed. Likewise, Victoria often produces excess electricity from solar and wind farms during the day, which could go to Tasmania. Related Article Energy Power struggle: Coalition pledge to scrap towers sparks bill warning The first stage is due for completion in 2030 and the second in 2033. In August last year, the Australian Energy Market Operator confirmed the project would cost about $7.57 billion for stages 1 and 2. Preparatory works have already begun at Sandy Point. Construction will involve a method known as horizontal directional drilling to install cable conduits under the beach at Waratah Bay. Nexa Advisory chief executive Stephanie Bashir said Marinus Link would form a crucial part of Australia’s energy infrastructure with enduring benefits and was worth the cost.

Advertisement

She said neither Victoria nor Tasmania could rely solely on the electricity they produced alone. While Victoria is currently a net exporter of electricity, Bashir said, the closure of coal-fired power stations from 2028 would result in Victoria needing to import electricity. “Our modelling shows that every year of delay, our bills go up,” she said. Nexa forecast average Victorian wholesale prices could increase up to 37 per cent between 2027 and 2031. Bashir said delaying projects like Marinus Link could cost Victorian households up to $472 over those four years. Grattan Institute energy and climate change deputy program director, Hamish McKenzie, said Marinus Link should theoretically keep power prices down in each state. More electric vehicles, data centres and households switching to electric appliances and heating are expected to drive up demand for power in coming years.

Advertisement

The closure of the Yallourn power station in 2028 is another factor set to reshape Victoria’s energy system. “We don’t have enough renewable generation to replace that,” McKenzie said. He said new transmission infrastructure would become increasingly important to meet Victoria’s electricity requirements. “If VNI West doesn’t proceed then Marinus Link becomes even more important,” McKenzie said.

Advertisement

Green Energy Markets chief executive Tristan Edis said Marinus Link was initially based on the idea that Tasmania would become the battery of the nation, but battery technology was now rolling out across Australia. “I do think we haven’t thoroughly evaluated other ways to solve those problems,” he said. Marinus Link has discussed with community groups local causes it can support. Among them is South Gippsland Landcare Network, which is seeking support to rehabilitate the Tarwin River catchment. Paul Peluso on one of his farm tracks. Joe Armao

Advertisement

Network chair Jillian Staton said Marinus Link should back local community and sport groups as part of its social licence, but Marinus Link should also leave a lasting environmental benefit. “Footy shirts are great, but this [Tarwin River] project is an opportunity for Marinus to have a positive long-term impact on the whole community,” she said. title: Buckley pulls out of North coach race as Lions board considers selection process
text:
Advertisement

Nathan Buckley has withdrawn from the race to become North Melbourne’s next senior coach, delivering a major twist in the Kangaroos’ search for Alastair Clarkson’s replacement. Two industry sources who spoke on the condition of anonymity confirmed to this masthead that Buckley had informed those involved in the process that he will not pursue the vacant position, ruling himself out of a return to senior coaching at Arden Street. Nathan Buckley splits his time as a Geelong assistant coach and Fox Footy analyst. AFL Photos Buckley was due to formally present to the coaching panel on Saturday, but told the club late last week that he would be removing himself from the process. It means Clarkson’s successor is set to be a first-time coach, with Daniel Giansiracusa, Jaymie Graham, David Hale and North assistant Xavier Clarke all in the mix.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘One of the hardest things I’ve done’: Three-time premiership coach Chris Fagan retires a Lions legend The Roos’ hunt for a new coach coincides with Brisbane’s, who need to replace retiring triple-premiership coach Chris Fagan. The Lions board will meet this week to decide whether to conduct a targeted process or throw the vacancy open to all candidates. Buckley had loomed as one of the most compelling candidates available to North as the club searches for the coach to lead its next era. His decision leaves the Kangaroos without one of the biggest names in the market and will force them to narrow their focus elsewhere as they continue the process of appointing Clarkson’s successor.

Advertisement

Buckley, 54, coached Collingwood for almost a decade, taking the club to the 2018 grand final and within a kick of a premiership, before stepping away in 2021 after 218 games in charge. He has since rebuilt his football profile through the media and repeatedly resisted opportunities to get back into the coaches’ box before joining the Cats as an assistant coach in 2026. Viney and club president Sonja Hood didn’t shy away from being frank about why they had sacked Clarkson Ruby Alexander The Kangaroos are searching for another coach after parting ways with Clarkson following four seasons in which the four-time premiership coach managed just 20 wins from 81 games. President Sonja Hood raised eyebrows in the media conference announcing Clarkson’s sacking by stating North needed a coach for the modern game.

Advertisement

North believed their young list had reached a point where it required a different voice and a coach suited to taking the group through the next phase of its development. Having already made the enormous call to move on from Clarkson, and having accumulated elite young talent through the draft, the Kangaroos are under pressure to get their next appointment right. Related Article Analysis

Trading and drafting On the market: Your team by team guide to AFL trade period The Kangaroos last week appointed three-time premiership Tiger Kane Lambert as head of development. Buckley’s decision to walk away from the North Melbourne opportunity after missing out on the top job with incoming side Tasmania suggests he is prepared to wait for the right job before returning as a senior coach.

Advertisement

He will continue as Chris Scott’s assistant at Geelong into 2027. North Melbourne and Buckley were contacted for comment. At Brisbane, the Lions have several strong internal candidates to consider as potential replacements for Fagan, who led the team to their third consecutive flag when they defeated Fremantle in the grand final. Brisbane Lions football manager Danny Daly is likely to be a candidate for the Lions’ vacant coaching position. AAP His long-time lieutenant Danny Daly is at the front of the queue, while assistant coach Cam Bruce is also a potential candidate, though the board will discuss which approach it takes to replace Fagan.

Advertisement

Bruce did his apprenticeship at the Hawks before becoming highly regarded at the Lions. Daly, who would need to be replaced as football manager if he were to take over from Fagan, started as an assistant coach at North Melbourne in 2003. He spent time at Richmond before joining the Lions in 2015, two seasons before Fagan’s appointment. He became football manager in 2021 but was Fagan’s eyes and ears in the coaches box on match day and indicated on SEN before last week’s grand final he had a desire to be a senior coach. Brisbane coach Chris Fagan is going out on a high with the club facing an unprecedented decision to replace him. AFL Photos via Getty Images “I’m not sure what life would be like without ‘Fages’ there so we might have to decide a few things myself. At the end of the day, it’s what’s best for the football club – whether that’s myself or a Cam Bruce, Dale Morris or getting someone new in,” Daly said. “That will be their decision and I’m happy with whatever they decide.”

Advertisement

Although Fagan had informed some key confidantes this would be his final season, the board had not been in a position to discuss a potential successor until the decision was official. Despite his success, Fagan was not among the highest-paid coaches in the game during his tenure, which enabled the Lions to fully resource the football department within the soft cap. It makes attracting an experienced coach – such as Adam Simpson and Buckley – or attempting to poach a current coach – such as former Lions premiership players Chris Scott (Geelong) or Craig McRae (Collingwood) – more unlikely than likely. The board could decide to look at a field of first-time coaches, which may include former Lion Murray Davis who is now at the Crows. Davis was interviewed for the Essendon coaching job won by Mark McVeigh. The Lions have not contacted external candidates directly.

Advertisement

Adelaide’s Matthew Nicks, St Kilda’s Ross Lyon, the Western Bulldogs’ Luke Beveridge and the Eagles’ Andrew McQualter are out of contract at the end of 2027. McQualter is a chance to have his contract extended before the start of next season. Only six coaches before Fagan have coached their team to a flag and not coached them the next season. Hawthorn’s Allan Jeans was the most recent, when the legendary coach handed over the reins to Alan Joyce for a season in 1989 due to ill health. The Hawks went back-to-back. Alex Jesaulenko left Carlton at the end of 1979 after a board upheaval and was replaced by Peter “Percy” Jones, while John Kennedy vacated the Hawks job in 1977 and handed it over to David Parkin on the eve of the 1978 season for family reasons. Neither team won the flag the next season.

Advertisement

Frank “Checker” Hughes was replaced at Melbourne by Allan La Fontaine in 1949 after a long coaching career at Richmond and Melbourne. Reg Hickey replaced Charlie Clymo after Clymo coached for one season for one premiership in 1931 while Charlie Ricketts vacated the post at South Melbourne after winning the 1909 flag. Lions CEO Sam Graham said on Thursday the club would announce its “next steps to appoint our next senior coach in due course”. The Lions retained their key players Logan Morris and Zac Bailey beyond this season. Lachie Neale has joined Collingwood as an unrestricted free agent while Sam Marshall has nominated St Kilda as his preferred destination.
