Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates – One morning in June, cryptocurrency mogul Changpeng Zhao pulled up to the St. Regis resort in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in a Nissan SUV. Zhao is the richest man in crypto, worth an estimated $US114 billion ($164 billion), and he lives in a villa nearby, with nine bedrooms, four bodyguards, a chef and a yacht. But he also likes to play the part of a “normal dude”, as he often describes himself, and that day he had offered to give me a personal tour of the city. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao was pardoned by US President Donald Trump last year after pleading guilty in 2023 to federal charges relating to violations of the American Bank Secrecy Act. Bloomberg Zhao, to be clear, isn’t a normal dude. Not long ago, US authorities brought a criminal case against him for his management of Binance, a crypto exchange depicted in court papers as a haven for Russian money launderers, Iranian sanctions evaders and Islamic State terrorists. Zhao pleaded guilty and escaped with his fortune intact. After serving a four-month prison sentence, he returned to Abu Dhabi, still Binance’s majority shareholder and still the most powerful figure in the industry. These days, Zhao, 49, moves through the world like a head of state, flying around Asia on his private jet to advise governments on crypto regulation. Zhao’s most influential allies are a pair of powerful ruling families. One is the clan that runs the UAE, which wants his help creating a technology powerhouse in the desert. The other is the Trumps.

Advertisement

Last year, Binance forged a business relationship with World Liberty Financial, the crypto start-up founded by US President Donald Trump and his three sons. World Liberty generated $US799 million for Trump last year — his single most lucrative asset. Trump pardoned Zhao last October, a move widely criticised as a quid pro quo. Known in the industry as “CZ”, Zhao often avoids reporters, but he met me several times this year, eager to put a friendlier gloss on his career at Binance, which still hasn’t stanched the flow of dirty money. For years, his true calling has been what academics term “jurisdictional arbitrage” — moving from country to country in search of a legal framework pliable enough to accommodate his appetite for risk and growth. In Abu Dhabi, he may have found an ideal base of operations. As we drove into the city, we passed a string of impressive compounds and drove towards the presidential palace, Qasr Al Watan, whose striking white dome resembles the Taj Mahal. Zhao was growing animated. “Democracy has been hailed as, like, the holy grail for the last couple hundred years, but democracies are inefficient,” he said. “If you get a benevolent dictator, it’s actually extremely efficient. There’s very little debate going on. You don’t waste time on a lot of frivolous stuff.” Related Article Analysis

US midterm elections America’s billionaires are turning their backs on Trump Lately, this top-down model of business and politics, simultaneously medieval and ultramodern, has gained traction in the United States. On a trip to Abu Dhabi last year, Trump called the nation’s ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, “a very strong man” and “a man of vision like few others”. Zach Witkoff, the son of one of Trump’s top advisers, put it more bluntly at a crypto conference in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, in May 2025. “We really need to take a page out of His Highness’ and the Emirates’ book,” Witkoff said. “They are just an amazing example of how you can lead with innovation while also maintaining your family values.”

Advertisement

One day early this year, Zhao was working when the windows began to shake. He got up and walked onto his balcony, where he saw a trail of smoke in the sky. Zhao lives on Saadiyat Island, an enclave of Abu Dhabi across the Persian Gulf from Iran, which had just fired a missile at the UAE. It was the start of a geopolitical crisis that has destabilised the region, but Zhao was not overly concerned. He returned to work. Billionaires gravitate to the UAE for billionaire reasons. The country doesn’t levy an income tax, and it’s considered extremely safe. Getty Images Until he settled in the UAE, Zhao was a man without a country. He was born in China, then moved to Canada with his family at the age of 12. After attending McGill University, he worked a series of technology jobs. In July 2013, over a poker game in Shanghai, a colleague suggested he check out “this new thing called bitcoin”. After a few months of study, Zhao made a radical bet. He sold the family home — a three-bedroom apartment in Shanghai where he and his wife were raising two children — and ploughed the $US900,000 in proceeds into bitcoin. Zhao went on to work at a succession of crypto start-ups in Asia. In July 2017, Zhao founded Binance. Within a few months, it was the largest exchange in the world, a title it has never relinquished. Binance’s success rested on two pivotal insights. The first was that crypto investors were drunk on risk and would never be satisfied swapping dollars or yen merely for an equivalent amount of crypto. For years, Binance has operated as a margin exchange: Traders can borrow money to place high-risk, high-reward bets on the prices of bitcoin and other popular tokens.

Advertisement

The second insight was simpler yet more consequential. Many crypto investors didn’t want to identify themselves, and Binance didn’t ask them to. For its first four years, the company allowed customers to open accounts without providing even the most basic KYC — the “know your customer” information that traditional companies require to prevent financial crime. The result was an extremely lucrative free-for-all: a platform where unvetted investment products were available to unvetted traders. As the market boomed, Binance took a cut of each transaction; the company quickly reached $US1 billion in profits, according to Zhao’s self-published memoir, Freedom of Money. Zhao was suddenly a crypto celebrity. But he has never been widely understood outside the industry. When he recounts his most contentious moments, Zhao portrays himself as a kind of passenger — a crypto nerd overwhelmed by success, a naive outsider. Related Article Billionaires Billionaire pardoned by Trump is back in the spotlight It is not always a convincing performance. In June, Zhao told me that he had “never really wanted” to break the law in Binance’s explosive early years, when the company’s lax controls allowed a procession of bad actors to launder money. “It’s just my lack of experience in that area,” he said. That image isn’t compatible with the evidence US prosecutors collected in their investigation into Binance. In court, they quoted an admonition that Zhao had given his underlings: “Better to ask for forgiveness than permission.” Privately, Zhao had discussed ways to obfuscate that Binance served American users even though it wasn’t licensed in the US, according to legal filings. “Don’t leave anything in writing,” he told a subordinate. Royal treatment

Advertisement

Zhao paid a visit to the UAE in 2021, after years of roaming around Asia. In 2017, he and his Binance colleagues had been forced to flee China, as the government prepared to announce a ban on crypto exchanges. A stint in Japan hadn’t worked out either, nor had Singapore. Then Zhao’s friend, Gabriel Abed, a businessperson who served as the ambassador to the UAE for Barbados, made a suggestion. He told Zhao to check out Dubai. Immediately, Zhao saw how the UAE treated the rich and powerful. He arrived in Dubai on a Saturday morning in October, and within hours, a government minister, Omar Sultan al-Olama, came to visit. He offered Zhao a so-called golden visa, which grants 10 years of hassle-free residency. A doctor was summoned to conduct the blood test required of all visa holders. Applications often take weeks to process; Zhao was approved in less than 12 hours. Not everyone in the UAE is treated so generously. Over the years, the nation’s leaders have conducted mass surveillance, outlawed even the mildest forms of dissent, and overseen a labor market where foreign workers are frequently exploited and abused. But for Zhao, it was the beginning of a comfortable new life. Before founding Binance, he had separated from his wife, who moved to Tokyo with their children. He started a relationship with one of his colleagues, He Yi, a marketing executive. While his older children attended college in the US, Zhao and He raised a young family in the UAE. Zhao got to know a group of Emirati leaders who were curious about technology. Eventually, he worked his way up to the brother of Sheikh Mohammed, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. During these early encounters, the sheikhs would pitch Zhao on the UAE, asking what they could do to help him. Soon, Zhao was preaching the nation’s virtues to the broader billionaire community. He encouraged artificial intelligence mogul Sam Altman to set up a corporate presence in the UAE, warning that other countries would treat him with hostility. UAE’s National Security Adviser Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan is a big backer of crypto. AP

title: On the market: Your team by team guide to AFL trade period
text:
Advertisement

The AFL trade period officially opens on Monday when the list managers from all the clubs gather at Marvel Stadium to get serious about the deals that will shape their teams for 2027. In truth, negotiations have been bubbling along for months for some players. The big questions are: Will Zach Merrett make it to Hawthorn at his second attempt? Will Gold Coast match Hawthorn’s free agency offer for Ben King and thereby force a trade? Where will Melbourne heart and soul player Jack Viney land? We examine every club and which players are on the market. Jesse Hogan, Rowan Marshall, Zach Merrett and Jack Viney are likely to feature in the trade period. Marija Ercegovac/Getty Images Follow our live blog every weekday during the trade period, which closes at 7.30pm on Wednesday, October 14. Adelaide

Advertisement

Draft picks: 13, 32, 33, 41, 54, 90

Key players: Nick Murray, Luke Pedlar The Crows were in the box seat for Zac Bailey, only for Bailey to remain a Lion on an eight-year deal. The Crows are set to lose Pedlar to Port Adelaide, but have a call to make on whether they trade key defender Murray, who has a five-year offer from North Melbourne. Murray, who has managed 78 games in six seasons with the Crows, including 11 this year, is contracted for another two seasons. Fellow tall backman Jordon Butts has already left for the Bulldogs in free agency. The Crows have been linked to Suns defender Charlie Ballard. Bigger picture, they are expected to make a play for St Kilda’s Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera and Hawthorn’s Will Day next year. - Jon Pierik Brisbane Lions Draft picks: 18, 39, 40, 51, 57, 77, 95

Key players: Keidean Coleman, Will McLachlan, Sam Marshall The Lions are likely to lose Marshall, who has requested a trade to St Kilda, while forward McLachlan has been linked with Essendon and Melbourne. Lachie Neale is off to Collingwood as a free agent, but Brisbane received only pick 39 as compensation, which will not help them match a bid on potential top-10 academy selection Caylen Murray. Out-of-favour defender Coleman is open to a fresh start at a different club. - Marc McGowan

Advertisement

Moving on: Star midfielder Lachie Neale has had a week of partying after the AFL grand final, but will soon be on his way to Collingwood. Getty Images Carlton Draft picks: 11, 16, 23, 24, 59, 70, 88 Key players: Hudson O’Keeffe, Flynn Riley The Blues have locked in ex-Swans key forward Joel Amartey through free agency, and their primary draft focus is matching a bid on Cody Walker, the son of former Blue Andrew Walker. Their top two selections in the draft add up to 2396 value index points, and they can also go into draft deficit, meaning they will have enough points to cover a bid up to No.2. Carlton also hope to land Giant Lachie Whitfield, while ex-Magpie Wil Parker will join as a delisted free agent. Ruckman O’Keeffe has requested a trade to the Western Bulldogs, while Riley is keen to move to the Magpies on a three-year deal. - Jon Pierik

Advertisement

Collingwood Draft picks: 9, 28, 66, 68, 75, 86

Key players: Scott Pendlebury, Dan Houston, Jordan De Goey, Harry DeMattia The Magpies are determined to remain in the premiership mix, and have landed three-time Brisbane premiership star Lachie Neale, who proved through a tumultuous 2026 campaign that his on-field output won’t be impacted by off-field headlines. A fourth-round pick will be enough to secure Giants forward Jesse Hogan, while they have met with Richmond’s rebounding defender Jayden Short. List boss Justin Leppitsch confirmed the Magpies were open to trading Jordan De Goey, who has a year left on his contract, but wants a long-term deal. Dan Houston’s future remains a point of interest, although he is contracted until the end of 2030 and his management has declared he is going nowhere. Scott Pendlebury will cross to Gold Coast. - Jon Pierik New colours: Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury will play for the Gold Coast Suns next year. Joe Armao Essendon

Advertisement

Related Article AFL 2026 Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft Draft picks: 1, 19, 60, 78

Key players: Zach Merrett, Jordan Ridley Again, the focus at Bomberland is Merrett, who, for the second-straight season, is seeking a trade to Hawthorn. As reported by this masthead, the Hawks have offered picks 15 and 25 in this year’s draft, along with a future selection – either a second- or third-round draft pick – but the Bombers have rebuffed this. It’s unclear what will satisfy Essendon when it comes to relinquishing their seven-time best-and-fairest, and former skipper. Merrett is contracted for 2027. The Bombers are chasing Melbourne premiership veteran Jack Viney, who could replace Merrett in the midfield. Defender Ridley is on Geelong and North Melbourne’s radar. Out-of-favour Cat Jack Bowes has requested a trade to the Bombers. - Jon Pierik Fremantle Draft picks: 17, 38, 58, 76, 94

Key players: Sean Darcy, Nathan O’Driscoll

Advertisement

Darcy’s future remains a point of debate despite the Dockers insisting the ruckman will remain at the club. He fell out of favour this season with Luke Jackson dominant, while Mason Cox was the preferred second ruck in their finals campaign. Darcy, 28, is contracted until the end of 2030. Wingman O’Driscoll has told the club he is exploring his options, having rejected a three-year contract offer amid interest from the Western Bulldogs. The Dockers say they have not expressed interest in luring ex-Magpie Bobby Hill or Sydney’s Chad Warner home, while their discussions with ex-Tiger Nathan Broad are purely about a coaching role. - Jon Pierik Geelong Draft picks: 14, 34, 55, 73, 91

Key players: Gryan Miers, Jack Bowes The Cats were disappointed to miss out on Zak Butters, but can now use that money to load up on other talent. Giants great Toby Greene officially joined on Friday as a free agent, while they are again haggling with the Saints over a trade for ruckman Rowan Marshall. The Cats have offered pick 32 as the crux of the deal, but St Kilda want Geelong’s top pick. The Cats are also chasing Essendon defender Jordan Ridley, and are open to discussing Nick Blakey, should the Swan be determined to leave the club after the alleged Pullman Hotel incident. Miers has completed a medical at West Coast, but remains keen to stay at Geelong, but Bowes has requested a trade to Essendon. - Jon Pierik Gold Coast

Advertisement

Draft picks: 65, 79, 83

Key players: Charlie Ballard, Ben King (restricted free agent), Jamarra Ugle-Hagan, Matt Rowell King will head to Hawthorn on a seven-year, $9 million deal, but the free agency compensation – pick No.7 – may not satisfy the Suns, who could match the Hawks’ offer and force a trade for the star goal-kicker. Hawk Aidan Schubert could end up being involved. Gold Coast have yet to indicate whether they will offer Ugle-Hagan another one-year deal, while Rowell is an intriguing case. The 2025 Brownlow medallist has a year to run on his contract, and is weighing up a return home to Victoria. If a sweetheart deal was put before the Suns now, would they move early? Gold Coast may need to engineer a late trade to secure unrestricted free agent Scott Pendlebury, so any compensation from the AFL for King is not diluted. Ballard is likely to stay at the club despite rival clubs’ interest. - Jon Pierik GWS Draft picks: 7, 26, 29, 48, 84

Key players: Harry Himmelberg, Jesse Hogan, Jake Stringer, Lachie Whitfield The Giants already decided not to offer contracts to Hogan and Kieren Briggs, and were comfortable with Stringer’s decision to move back to Victoria, but were hoping to retain Toby Greene, who is off to Geelong. Whitfield is poised to become a Blue after completing a medical after GWS were open to shedding his salary as they prioritise their younger group. A fourth-round pick will seal Hogan’s passage to Collingwood early in the trade period, while Briggs joined Richmond on a four-year deal. GWS may look to add more ruck depth and had explored interest in Bulldogs big man Tim English. - Marc McGowan

Advertisement

Hawthorn Draft picks: 15, 25, 27, 35, 69, 92

Key players: Sam Butler, Finn Maginness, Will McCabe, Noah Mraz, Max Ramsden, Aidan Schubert, Jack Scrimshaw They already had some wins when in-demand duo Bailey Macdonald and Calsher Dear re-signed. Ben King and Zach Merrett will be Hawks by the end of the player movement period, but how those deals look remains to be seen. North’s Josh Goater has also requested a trade to Hawthorn. Gold Coast are publicly threatening to match any Hawks free agency offer for King, which would trigger a trade, but that is to be determined – and could impact what Hawthorn can offer Essendon for Merrett. The Bombers are trying to convince the Hawks to include developing defender Mraz in any Merrett deal, but Hawthorn are adamant that won’t happen. Fringe players Butler (West Coast) and Maginness (Western Bulldogs) have opposition interest. - Marc McGowan Melbourne Draft picks: 6, 10, 47, 87

Key players: Trent Rivers, Jack Viney

Advertisement

The Demons missed out on Hawk Calsher Dear, who decided to stay in brown and gold. However, once-prized Roo Zane Duursma wants to join Steven King’s squad and that deal will require some haggling to determine his current value after being the No.4 pick in 2023. Lion Will McLachlan is another possible addition. Viney played just once this past season due mostly to injury, but Melbourne are going in a different midfield direction and encouraged him to explore his options. West Coast and Essendon are duelling for Viney’s signature, and it is unlikely he will net a strong return as effectively a salary dump. Rivers was once considered a big part of Melbourne’s future, but there have been constant murmurings that he might pursue a fresh start this off-season, which is yet to eventuate. - Marc McGowan Jack Viney in action recently. AFL Photos North Melbourne Draft picks: 5, 45, 64, 72, 82

Key players: Zane Duursma, Josh Goater, Tom Powell The Kangaroos’ No.1 off-season target is contracted Adelaide key defender Nick Murray, who they have presented with a five-year contract. That deal rests on the Crows’ willingness to let him go, and what North would offer to tempt them to relinquish defensive depth. Powell is a South Australian, so is often raised a potential part of any Murray trade. Duursma wants to join Melbourne, while Goater is keen to be a Hawk, so the Roos can expect to be busy in this year’s trade period. Contracted Bomber Jordan Ridley is a target, but his preference is believed to be Geelong. They were also keen on Cat Jack Bowes, but he nominated Essendon instead. Could they pivot to players such as Hawthorn’s Jack Scrimshaw and/or Max Ramsden? - Marc McGowan

Advertisement

Port Adelaide Draft picks: 4, 22, 30, 44, 46, 63, 81

Key players: Tom Anastasopoulos, Zak Butters, Ollie Lord, Todd Marshall Butters is the big one here, and specifically, what the Power will garner from his impending move to the Western Bulldogs. They will score pick five if they choose not to match the Dogs’ enormous nine-year deal, worth up to $18 million. That scenario remains a likely outcome, even after the AFL blocked their proposed side trade that involved Marshall also heading to the Kennel, Port paying a large chunk of his salary, and scoring two first-round picks in return. However, league rules prohibit a club losing a free agent from paying the salary of another player going to the same club, for integrity reasons. It is still probable that Marshall is in different colours next year, with both parties open to a move. Crow Luke Pedlar wants to join the Power. - Marc McGowan Richmond Draft picks: 2, 20, 42, 61

Key players: Jayden Short

Advertisement

The Tigers have already bolstered their ruck division with the free agency addition of ex-Giant Kieren Briggs, after they initially pursued his teammate Nick Madden. Briggs inked a four-year deal that positions himself as Richmond’s long-term successor for captain Toby Nankervis. Short is exploring his trade options, including meeting with Collingwood, but this masthead previously confirmed that fellow veteran Nick Vlastuin is not interested in continuing his career elsewhere. They did attempt to recruit Zak Butters, but were never considered as a genuine frontrunner. The Tigers will bring in another top talent in the draft and may be involved in some peripheral trades across the next 10 days. - Marc McGowan St Kilda Draft picks: 8, 49, 67, 85

Key players: Rowan Marshall, Mattaes Phillipou, Alix Tauru St Kilda’s Alix Tauru is talented but raw. Getty Images Fringe Lion Sam Marshall has requested a trade to the Saints, who continue to add secondary players from other clubs as they try to return to the finals. Marshall wanted to join Geelong last year and is again pursuing that move, which should eventuate this time. The Cats have so far knocked back St Kilda’s interest in Lawson Humphries and Sam De Koning, while they are also reluctant to part with their first-round selection. The Tauru saga is a fascinating one, and could still have another twist, but the likeliest outcome is he remains a Saint. Another of St Kilda’s top-10 picks, Phillipou, who is reportedly on a $1 million-a-year salary, was raised in trade dispatches, but club football boss Lenny Hayes denied he was up for grabs. Hayes also revealed it was unlikely they would broker a trade for Bulldog Rory Lobb. - Marc McGowan

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Focus on ex-Dees skipper heats up as Dons, Eagles fight it out; Dogs land defensive help for flag tilt Sydney Swans Draft picks: 36, 37, 50, 52, 74, 93

Key players: Nick Blakey Key forward Joel Amartey has already left in free agency for Carlton after the Swans traded for ex-Blue Charlie Curnow a year ago. That netted Sydney a second-round pick as compensation. The Blakey situation will remain a talking point until it gets shut down. Blakey, who is contracted for five more seasons on a lot of money, is believed to be open to a move to Geelong, but this is a complex situation and any potential deal would require the Cats giving up something significant. - Marc McGowan West Coast

Advertisement

Draft picks: 3, 21, 43, 56, 62, 71, 80

Key players: N/A The Eagles are actively pursuing talent to hasten their rebuild, with Jack Viney, Gryan Miers and Sam Butler among the opposition players on their wish list. They are in a two-way battle with Essendon for Viney, while they have undertaken medical testing on Miers, but he ideally wants to stay at Geelong. Hawthorn’s Butler has never played more than nine games in a season, so could be keen on a fresh start, but is contracted for one more season. Melbourne’s Trent Rivers, who hails from Western Australia and is rumoured to be considering his options, could emerge as a target if he requests a trade from the Demons. - Marc McGowan Western Bulldogs Draft picks: 12, 31, 53, 89

Key players: Tim English, Rory Lobb The Bulldogs already signed ex-Crows defender Jordon Butts in free agency, and superstar midfielder Zak Butters is also headed their way, whether in restricted free agency or a trade with Port Adelaide in a major coup. A proposed side deal in Butters negotiations that would have seen the Power send Todd Marshall to the Dogs and pay a chunk of his salary in return for two first-round picks won’t happen. However, Marshall could still find his way to Luke Beveridge’s club – just not in that exact fashion. Out-of-favour Hawk Finn Maginness, who is contracted for 2027, is on the Bulldogs’ radar, while Docker Nathan O’Driscoll could be a name to follow. Ruckman English is expected to remain at the club for next season, while St Kilda have indicated any deal for Lobb was unlikely. - Marc McGowan Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
